It signifies the solicitude and diligence that greater and lesser prelates of churches ought to have concerning the upbringing of their subjects in doctrine and their salvation. Galatians 4: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'

Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'as though Paul had given birth to the whole world, so did he hasten to bring all into the kingdom of God, by teaching, by promising, now by prayer, now by supplication, for them.'

Tenth, as blessed Ambrose says in the Hexameron: they have an extraordinary devotion toward raising their young; and, in proportion to how much time they spend on them, so much are they, in turn, nourished by their own young in their old age.

They signify that we ought to honor and cherish our parents, and remember their kindnesses, especially in time of need. 'You shall honor your mother all the days of your life; for you ought to remember what and how great dangers she suffered for you in her own womb.'
'Honor God, and your parents, and, as though to masters, serve those who begot you, in every deed and word.'
Jerome, in a certain letter: 'love the head of the monastery as a father, cherish him as a teacher, believe whatever he tells you.'

Eleventh, as the author puts it: 'although they eat frogs, and snakes, and other venomous things of this kind, the venom nonetheless does not overcome or change their nature; hence it becomes for them refreshment and nourishment, which is, to men and to many other creatures, poison. For, by the force of the heat that dominates within them, the power of the venom is extinguished and overcome.'

They signify that evil things do not harm the good, who are not overcome by evil, but, through the power of charity growing warm in the soul, overcome evil with good, according to that saying of the Apostle, Romans 12.
An example is found in blessed John the Evangelist, who, as is found in his Life, drank poison, and it did him no harm at all.
Augustine, in the book of Retractations: 'nothing can harm the just man.'

As Ambrose puts it in the Hexameron: storks fly across the sea, and, gathering in formation, fly together to warmer regions. In their descent, however, they have crows as companions, which go before them, and, as it were, providing an escort for the storks in their ranks, join together in troops, and, fighting against other birds hostile to the storks, take upon themselves, at their own peril, wars not their own.

It signifies that the wicked sometimes serve the good, and secular men, religious, in this pilgrimage of the world. Acts 28: 'but the barbarians showed us no small kindness. For, kindling a fire, they refreshed us all, because of the rain that was falling, and the cold.' An example is found in that robber who is said to have attended blessed Mary and her child in the doubtful forest, when they were fleeing into Egypt.

As the same author says, when their chicks are born, their legs, feet, and beak are very black, like a swan's; but, laying aside their blackness little by little, they begin to grow red, the more they grow old.

They signify men who are all born children of wrath, because of original sin, but who, through baptism, become children of grace and of twofold charity, and, the more they advance in age, the more they progress in virtue and goodness, and in that same twofold charity: 'we were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest; but God, who is rich in mercy, because of his exceeding great love, has quickened us together in Christ, and has raised us up together, by whose grace we are saved.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: 'it is the property of virtue always and continually to progress.'
The crow, or little crow, is found to have these conditions, or properties.
A garrulous and wicked bird, very harmful to the inhabitants of the place where it dwells.

It signifies men who are harmful to their neighbors, or gossiping and clamorous women, or quarrelsome and merciless ones, who bring scandal into the neighborhood. Proverbs 9: 'a foolish woman, and clamorous, and full of allurements, and knowing nothing at all; she sits at the door of her house, to call to those passing by, and going on their way.'
Origen, in the homily On the Canaanite Woman: 'woman, the head of sin, the weapon of the devil, the expulsion from paradise, the corruption of the old law.'
'By a woman sin had its beginning, and through her we all die.' 'It is better to dwell with a lion and a dragon, than to keep house with a wicked woman.'
Second, as the same author says, it feeds on unclean and poisonous things.
It signifies the lustful, who delight in uncleanness under the pretext of carnal sweetness.
They acquire for themselves the poison of everlasting death. Proverbs 5: 'the lips of a harlot are a dripping honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood.'
Gregory, in the book of Dialogues: 'punishment will open the eyes that guilt now closes.'
Third, as the same author puts it, it lives a very long time, and, in old age, turns white in its feathers; but the older it grows, the blacker it becomes inwardly, in its flesh.

It signifies evil men who, in old age, seem to wish to amend themselves, and pretend they wish to be cleansed and renewed from their vices and sins, but, as regards the truth of the matter, die in their iniquities, always growing in evil. Isaiah 65: 'the child shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner being a hundred years old shall be accursed.' An example is found in the elders of Susanna.
'Grown old in evil days,' Daniel 13.
Blessed Gregory also gives an example, in book 3 of the Dialogues, of Ludoildus, king of the Goths, who indeed recognized that our faith was true, but in the end did not merit to attain salvation.
Fourth, as the same author says, it hates the fox more than any other animal, and strives, wherever it can attack it, to gouge out or peck at its eyes.

It signifies, in this, the good man supremely detesting the devil, and the company of heretics, and every counsel and council of the wicked. Psalm 25: 'I have hated the assembly of the malignant, and with the wicked I will not sit.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus, Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: Seneca, to Lucilius: 'the first step of innocence is to hate wicked things.'

Fifth, as the same author says, it is marvelously and persistently hostile to the eagle and to all birds of prey. For it pursues and harasses the eagle, which it fears to touch, with cries and flight, yet it does not always profit from its own wickedness, since, after the eagle's long forbearance, it is sometimes struck and killed by the eagle's beak, when it comes closer than it ought.

It signifies those who are rebellious against their prelates and superiors, in words and in opposing positions, who, even if they are borne along for a time, are nonetheless finally judged by God, when they do not repent.

An example is found in Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who so conducted themselves against Moses and Aaron, and at last went down alive into hell, with their households and their goods, covered by the earth, as is found in Numbers 16.

An example among the monks of blessed Bernard, in the monastery of Clairvaux, who, as is found in the accounts of his deeds, stirring up a multitude against their father and not repenting, and boldly approaching holy communion, then heard, secretly, from blessed Bernard: 'I indeed give you the sacrament, but I have no doubt at all that you will feel, and bear, a heavenly judgment.'

Sixth, as blessed Ambrose says in the Hexameron: crows escort and guide storks across the sea, and, as it were, joining themselves in troops around them like an escort, engage in battle against other birds hostile to the storks, taking upon themselves, at their own peril, wars not their own. A sign of this is that, at the time when the storks fly across the sea, crows are not found in their usual places; and that, when they return wounded, they show, by a certain evident cry of blood and by other signs, that they have undergone a grave struggle of battles.
These things signify that the secular sometimes profit the religious, according to that saying, Ecclesiasticus 4: 'be affable to the congregation of the poor.'
And that the good expose themselves to danger for the salvation of others, 1 John 2: 'Christ has laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De diligendo Deo Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, On the Love of God: 'for holy men, all flesh is an instrument of good work.'

Seventh, as the same blessed Ambrose says there: this bird's compassion toward its parents is admirable. For when it happens that they are diminished, through long old age, in the covering of their feathers and the governance of their wings, the younger crows warm them with their own feathers, and feed them with food they have gathered. And when their parents grow old, they raise them up with the support of their own wings, and exercise them for flying, so as to call back and restore their loosened limbs to their former use.

They clearly signify how great, and of what kind, ought to be the piety and diligence of men toward their parents and their prelates, or superiors, especially in old age and in time of need. Ecclesiasticus 3: 'he that fears God honors his parents, and will serve them that begot him as his masters, in every deed and word.'
Jerome, in a certain letter: 'love the head of the monastery as a father; cherish him as a teacher; believe whatever he tells you.'
The raven is found, according to the authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: For first, as Gregory says in the Moralia, and Isidore likewise, it looks at the gaping mouths of its young, to whom it does not first give food, unless it first recognizes, through the blackness of their feathers, a likeness to its own color; once it sees them growing black, it then feeds them with all its strength.

It signifies worldly men, who are unwilling to love or cherish any but those like themselves. John 7: 'the world cannot hate you; but me it hates, because I give testimony of it, that its works are evil.'
Chrysostom, in the sermon for the third Sunday of Lent: 'the wicked cannot bear to see what is good; so the life of the good is a torment to the very worst.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Enarrationes in Psalmos Augustini
Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Second, as Augustine says on the Psalms, and Gregory in the Moralia, and Isidore: the young ravens are said to be fed by heavenly dew, as long as their feathers have not yet blackened; once that has happened, they are fed by their parents.

They signify that the grace of God nourishes innocent ravens, that is, Christ's poor, living innocently in religion and given to the practice of prayer. Job 39: 'who provides food for the raven, when her young ones cry to God, wandering about, because they have no food?'
'The beasts of burden, the young ravens.'

Ambrose, on that verse of 2 Corinthians 4, as is found in the continuous Gloss: 'we are made poor, but not destitute; sometimes we come to such poverty that even the necessities of life are often lacking, but we are not destitute, since in the end God comes to our aid, and helps us.'
The raven seeks out the hidden places of corpses among the dead.

It signifies that detractors, or slanderers, gladly search out the hidden faults of the good, unknown to others; against which, Psalm 100: 'him that detracted secretly against his neighbor, I persecuted.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, in a certain sermon on the Song of Songs: 'they are tormented at the good deeds of their elders, and feed on their evil ones.'
Fourth, as Fulgentius says, in a certain treatise of his, it is a noisy bird, forming various sounds. For the raven alone, among birds, has changes of voice.

It signifies whisperers, and those who twist and change their words. Proverbs 26: 'an enemy is known by his lips, when in his heart he has contrived deceit. When he shall speak low, trust him not, for there are seven mischiefs in his heart.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'You may see them walk apart, come together, sit down together, and shameless birds let loose their tongues.'
Fifth, as Isidore says, it is a deceitful bird, stealing things and hiding them away in remote and secret places.
It signifies thieves, and the deceitful, and the greedy. Habakkuk 2: 'woe to him that heaps together what is not his own; how long does he load himself with thick clay?'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on 'if any man will come after me': 'for what did the old, carnal man know, but to seize the goods of others, if he could?' and so on.
As the same Isidore says, it is a bird that settles on corpses, and seeks its food among venomous and unclean things.
It signifies carnal and brutish men, given over to acts of lust and the uncleanness of the flesh, and rotting away in them. Joel 1: 'the beasts of burden have rotted in their own dung.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'for beasts of burden to rot in their own dung is for carnal men to end their life in the stench of lust.'
'The raven, the crow.'

It signifies the wise of this world, always intent on novelties, and given to curious things, and reckoning themselves, as it were, singular and unique in the world. Acts 17: 'now all the Athenians, and the strangers dwelling there, employed themselves in nothing else but either to tell or to hear some new thing.'
Augustine, in the Confessions, and elsewhere: 'the human race is a curious kind, eager to know the life of another, but slow to know its own.'
The raven fights with the donkey and with the bull, flying over them, and harming them, striking with its beak, and pecking at their eyes.

It signifies those who attack simple and dull persons, lacking understanding or good sense. Proverbs 28: 'as a roaring lion, and a hungry bear, so is a wicked ruler over the poor people; a leader void of prudence shall oppress many by his power.'
The Gloss, on that verse of Psalm 39, 'but I am a beggar and poor': 'to pursue the poor is the height of savagery.'
Ninth, as Aristotle says in book 7, the female ravens brood over the eggs alone, and the males bring them food.
They signify Job 21: 'why do the wicked live, are they advanced, and strengthened with riches? Their seed continues before them, a multitude of kinsmen, and of children's children, in their sight.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Against which, Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'
The black raven is a friend to the fox, and defends it from beasts hostile to it.
This signifies that there is a certain love among the wicked, and a mutual familiarity. Proverbs 13: 'he that walks with the wise shall be wise; but a friend of fools shall become like them.'
Ecclesiasticus 13: 'every animal loves its like.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'you may see the whisperer go apart, come together, sit down together, and soon let loose shameless tongues to speak whispered slander. One is joined to one,' and so on.

Eleventh, as the same Aristotle says there, ravens fight a fierce battle, and strike one another with their weapons, that is, with their beaks, their talons, and their wings, and the loser obeys the victor, by the force of the victory.

They signify men in disagreement over business, or even opposing advocates, overcoming one another rationally, or prevailing at law, and wisely coming to agreement in the end. Job 34: 'let us choose judgment among ourselves, and let us see between ourselves what is best.'
Since Job said, 'I am just,' and God has overthrown my judgment.
Augustine, in book 4 of the Confessions: 'a few dissensions make one great agreement.'
The raven, in the midst of summer's heat, contrary to the nature of other birds, lays eggs and rears its young.

It signifies that, in a time of tribulation, the good especially advance, and multiply works meritorious for eternal life. 2 Corinthians 12: 'for when I am weak, then I am powerful, for strength is made perfect in weakness.'

An example is found in a certain leprous holy father, blessed Jerome relates, to whom money was offered, and who answered the one offering it: 'do you wish to take from me the God who has fed me for seventy years without money?' And he did not accept it. He also tells of another who lamented that, whereas he had been sick in other years, in one year he had not been sick, and grieved greatly over this.
The cuckoo is found, according to experienced men, or the authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as Pliny says, it is beautiful, with varied plumage, but wretched.
It signifies those, according to Proverbs, who have bodily beauty without uprightness or goodness: 'favor is deceitful, and beauty is vain; the woman that fears the Lord, she shall be praised.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus, Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: Juvenal: 'true nobility is that which virtue makes, and which adorns the soul with character.' Seneca, in letter 45: 'that man is noble whom nature has well suited for virtue.'
Second, as the same Aristotle says, it is weak in its feet, as is clear when it sits on a tree.

It signifies, according to Proverbs, certain men noble in appearance and in outward sense, but base in their inward affections and dispositions: 'as a golden ring in a swine's snout, so is a beautiful woman without discretion.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus, Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Against which, Chrysostom, on Matthew, homily 44: 'there is one true nobility, namely, to do the will of God.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, to Eugenius, book 1: 'the lineage of the apostles is noble by nothing else than the nobility of their character.'

bibl.author: Valerius Maximus, Facta et dicta memorabilia Valerii Maximi

cit.quote: Socrates, born of a midwife mother and a stone-mason father, rose to the brightest light of glory, the best teacher of life.

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus, Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: Seneca: 'philosophy made Plato noble,' and his own excellent natural gifts made Aristotle noble.
Martianus: it has a furtive and sluggish gait, or flight, and always stays near the ground.

It signifies hypocrites and heretics, who always walk by two paths, feigning, or pretending, an appearance of maturity. Ecclesiasticus 2: 'woe to the double heart, and to wicked lips, and to the hands that do evil, and to the sinner that walks on the earth two ways.'
'Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke, and elsewhere: 'feigned fairness is not fairness, but a twofold iniquity.'

...a bird; for it never makes a nest, since it is loath to labor, and instead invades nests made by other, lesser birds, and eats eggs not its own. Moreover, though it has by nature the task of purging gardens of the caterpillars, or grubs, on which it most gladly feeds, even if it begins to do so, it at once turns away. It signifies certain base men who are of such negligence and laziness that they are unwilling to profit or labor, but prefer to consume the labors of others.

And they so love the belly's ease that they refuse to exercise even the gifts freely given them by God or by nature, and prefer to waste away within themselves. Proverbs 20: 'because of the cold, the sluggard would not plow; he shall beg, therefore, in the summer, and it shall not be given him.'
'The sluggard hides his hands under his armpits, and it is a labor to him to bring them to his mouth.'
'The disdain of a sluggard for oxen,' or 'for labor.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Letam de institutione filie

cit.quote: Jerome, to Laeta, On the Education of a Daughter: 'for it is easy to be a rival of evils.'
And again, to Nepotian: 'always be doing something, so that the devil may find you occupied.'
...a bird of decent size, yet of great foolishness; for it flees the cicada, and fears birds far smaller than itself that pursue it.

It signifies certain men who appear great, dove-like, in stature or in person, and yet are fainthearted and lacking in heart when it comes to boldness and effectiveness. Hosea 7: 'Ephraim has become like a deceived dove, without heart.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: The Canon; and: 'he is to be reckoned most base, unless he excel in knowledge and goodness, who excels in honor.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus, Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: 'That man is noble whom nature has well disposed toward virtue.'

Sixth, as Martianus says, when it perceives its own song being mocked by a man imitating it, in matching voice and manner, after some pretense of ignoring it, it abandons its natural call and, multiplying its voice, mocks that man as though in insult, and inveighs against the one mocking it.

It signifies those who are impatient at the words, or even the jests, of others; against which, Romans 15: 'we that are stronger ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves. For Christ did not please himself, but, as it is written, the reproaches of them that reproached you fell upon me.'
'To know how to overlook a thing, as time and place require, is the highest prudence.'
'Patience is a noble kind of conquering; he who suffers, conquers,' and so on.
As the same author says, it gives out a great cry, multiplied and continued in uniform calls, without any resulting fruit.

It signifies certain wise men, or would-be scholars, of this age, who make a show, in words, of being capable of anything, and boast likewise in promises and displays, and yet are worth nothing in effective deeds — to whom applies that saying, Proverbs 14: 'where there are many words, there is oftentimes want.'
'Clouds, and wind, and no rain — such is the boastful man that does not fulfill his promises.'
An example is found in Simon Magus, who, as is found in the Itinerary, was more in words than in deeds, more in display than in substance, more in promising than in paying.
Eighth, as Pliny says, and as experience proves, its flesh is saffron-colored, as it were, and tasty enough, but of little benefit, or healthfulness, and little sought after.

It signifies the delights of this age, which appear pleasing and lovable to the wanton and the imprudent, but are, in the end, harmful and embittering. Proverbs 5: 'the lips of a harlot are a dripping honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood.'
For the delights of sinners are always followed by the bitterness of torments, as is found in Amos 5: 'your feast days,' and so on.
Ninth, as Isidore puts it, cuckoos are carried from Spain into Italy on the backs of kites, because of the weakness of their own flight.

This signifies that the rich and powerful of this age ought to relieve the burdens of the poor and the wretched, in their time of need. 1 Timothy, last chapter: 'charge the rich of this world to give easily, to communicate, to lay up treasure,' and so on.
The Ordinary Gloss: 'to give easily, that is, to reckon as common what they have, is to lay up temporal things in the treasury of heaven.'
The swan is found to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as Isidore says, it is entirely white in its feathers; for no one has ever found it black.
It signifies a man of evangelical, or virginal, chastity. Apocalypse 3: 'you have a few names in Sardis, who have not defiled their garments; they shall walk with me in white, for they are worthy.'
It is sung of blessed Dominic: 'keeping the flower of modesty unstained, he attained the celibacy of an exalted life'; and again, 'preserving without stain the lily of virginity,' and so on.

Second, as the same Isidore says, the swan ('cygnus') is named from singing ('canendo'), since it has a sweet song, and makes use of modulated and varied voices; it is also said that, in the Hyperborean mountains, or regions, belonging to lyre-players, cygnets fly out of their nests and sing together fittingly, in harmony, as the same Isidore says.

These signify contemplative men, each rejoicing on his own, above the level of the mind, and all together, in the eternal God. Psalm 94: 'come, let us rejoice in the Lord, let us make a joyful noise to God our savior.'
'Blessed is the people that knows the joyful shout' — that is, that experiences the sweetness of the eternal harmony.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Enarrationes in Psalmos Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, on the Psalms: 'a hymn is [praise] of God, together with song.'
As blessed Ambrose says in the Hexameron, sailors reckon it a good omen when swans are met with in a shipwreck.
The swan is always a most joyful bird in omens; sailors, too, wish for it, since it does not sink beneath the waves, and so it was consecrated to Apollo, as Martianus says.

It signifies that the presence of good men, like Stephanas and Fortunatus, gladdens the afflicted. 1 Corinthians, last chapter: 'I rejoice in the presence of Stephanas and Fortunatus, since what was wanting on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed both my spirit and yours.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Epistola Augustini ad Probam

cit.quote: 'Let good men be present, and all sorrows are lightened and made bearable.'
As Martianus says, its greatest strength is in its wings.
It signifies that the uprightness of the saints lies in the strength of their virtues. Song of Songs, last chapter: 'I am a wall, and my breasts are as a tower.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Dionysius, in the book On the Angelic Hierarchy: 'the conditions of the purity of the spirits above are that, according to their most excellent chastity, they are set above by their most godlike virtues, and, toward those beneath them, know nothing at all of contempt.'

Fifth, as the same Martianus says, when the swan is in love, it seeks out the female, and coaxes her by the embrace of its neck, and, as it were, draws her toward itself, joining its neck to hers by encircling it. After coupling, however, the female strikes the male and drives him off. But the male bathes himself after coupling, and likewise the female, before taking food.

It signifies the love of married people, and that good married couples cleanse themselves with tears and alms, according to the counsel of Daniel 4: 'redeem your sins with alms, and your iniquities with works of mercy to the poor; perhaps God will forgive your offenses.'
Ambrose, in the sermon On Blessed Peter's Chains: 'tears wash away the fault which shame forbids the voice to confess.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: As blessed Ambrose puts it, in the Hexameron, and on Luke: at the approach of death, with a feather fixed into its brain, it sings, and, contrary to the custom of other animals, it then gives forth song instead of a groan.
It signifies holy men rejoicing and exulting in death, from the consideration of the end of their present misery, and their ascent to the rewards of the eternal homeland.

An example is found in Simeon, the venerable old man of the Gospel, Luke 2, who, with death approaching, having seen and adored and carried the incarnate Word, sang to God, saying: 'now you dismiss your servant, O Lord, in peace.'

Blessed Jerome also gives an example, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, of abbot Sisoes, who, as he was dying, had his face radiate with a certain brightness, since blessed Anthony, already dead, had come to him; afterward his whole face glowed red, since the choirs of the prophets had come upon him; afterward, his countenance shining with the brightness of the sun, at the presence of Christ, he said: 'in truth, I have not yet even felt the beginning of penance, so great is the glory of the penitent.' And that whole place was filled with a pleasant fragrance, as he flew away, rejoicing, to the heavens.
It has the whitest plumage, unmixed with any color or blackness at all, but its flesh is black, and hard to digest.

It signifies hypocrites, gracious on the outside, but wicked within, and deprived of God's grace. Matthew 23: 'woe to you, hypocrites, who are like whitened sepulchers, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but within are full of filth and all uncleanness.'
Ambrose, in the sermon On the Lord's Passion: 'every pretense, and every duplicity, is a lie.'
'These shall receive the greater damnation.'
...fish. It does not eat fish; rather, if bread or food is thrown to it, it leaves it to the fish that follow it, and seeks its own living from grasses and roots.

It signifies that good men ought not to injure their neighbors, but to be beneficial to them, and humbly content with their own state. Exodus 2, and Acts 7: 'sirs, you are brothers; why do you wrong one another?'
'He gave a command to every one of them concerning his neighbor.'
'And having food, and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content.'

'You did not yet know my life: bread with olives, and rarely even with vegetables, is my usual food. As for clothing, this that you see — a tunic with a cloak — and having this, I seek nothing else. This is enough for me, since my mind aspires not to these present things, but to the eternal, and so nothing among present, visible things delights me.'

Ninth, as blessed Ambrose says in the Hexameron, it has feet that are black, broad, and webbed, very well suited for swimming, one of which it uses like an oar, in swimming, and the other like a rudder, to steer itself.

It signifies the progress, in affection, in merit, and in discretion of life, of a spiritual or religious man, humble in his own estimation. 1 Timothy 3: 'these things I write to you, son Timothy, hoping that I shall come to you shortly; but if I tarry long, that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God.'
Chrysostom, On Paul: 'Paul did nothing idly, but did all things with a just and probable reason, openly, and at the fitting time.'
As the same Ambrose says, it dwells in ponds and lakes, and nests near the water, where, on a few sticks gathered together at once, it broods over its eggs together, and raises its young.

It signifies that those eager for heavenly wisdom dwell by the streams of the venerable Scriptures, in which, placing their devotion, they bring forth sacred thoughts, and, with the whole affection of their soul, raise up merits for eternal life.

Jeremiah 17: 'blessed is the man that trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence. And he shall be as a tree that is planted by the waters, that spreads out its roots toward moisture, and shall not fear when the heat comes; and it shall not be anxious in the time of drought, neither shall it cease at any time to bring forth fruit.'

'I exhort you not to be reluctant to devote care to the truly and certainly holy Scriptures; I especially exhort you to read the tongues of the apostles. For by these you will be stirred to know the prophets, whose testimonies the apostles use.'

It diligently nourishes and raises its young, and protects and defends them with beak and hiss. And if anyone approaches against them, it never ceases to set itself against him, and to interpose itself.

It signifies the diligence and solicitude that prelates ought to have concerning their subjects, in raising them in Christ and defending them from the danger of adversaries. 2 Corinthians 12: 'most gladly will I spend, and be spent myself, for your souls.'
'I became, in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishing her children.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, speaking to prelates: 'suspend the blows, bring forth the breasts. Show yourselves as mothers in cherishing, as fathers in correcting.'
Galatians 4: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again,' and so on.
'Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?'
...a bird of great fleshiness and bodily weight, and so it loves rest, and rarely flies, as Martianus puts it.
It signifies the carnal, and the given-to-pleasure, or the delicate, unfit for contemplation. Philippians 3: 'whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with earthly vanities cannot know divine things.'
But wild ones fly with strong flight, their necks stretched out and their feet applied to the rear. But they are not so great in body, nor so plump, as the tame ones raised near the dwellings of men.

They signify religious, or hermits, wholly given over to God through contemplation, despising the world and worldly things with their whole will and action. 'Forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before, I press toward the mark, for the prize of the supernal calling of God in Christ Jesus.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'he to whom God is his portion ought to care for nothing but God.'
The gnat is found to have these conditions, or properties.

For first, as Isidore says, it is a very small and tiny fly, named from its sting, since it sucks blood. It has, in its mouth, a tube like a goad, with which it pierces the flesh, so as to drink the blood.
It signifies detractors, shedding the blood of their neighbors. Proverbs 1: 'their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood.'
'He who plots evil against his neighbor pierces the side of Christ with a lance.'
'Whoever is prompt and swift to run to evil afflicts the hands of Christ with nails.' Ecclesiastes 10: 'dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment.'
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is counted among flying things, like the bee, even though its body is that of a worm having many feet, since it has wings by which it flies.

It signifies hypocrites, who are counted among the good and among those seeking heavenly things, and yet, in truth, are numbered among wretched and baser men. 2 Corinthians 11: 'for such false apostles are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ. And no wonder: for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. It is no great thing, therefore, if his ministers be transformed as the ministers of righteousness, whose end shall be according to their works.'
Ambrose, in the sermon On the Lord's Passion: 'every pretense, and every duplicity, is a lie.'
Isidore: it is generated from putrid vapors, from corpses, and from corrupted marshy places.

It signifies carnal men, drawing the beasts of their own carnality from the stench of lust and gluttony, and rotting away in it, according to that saying, Joel 1: 'the beasts of burden have rotted in their own dung.'
Isaiah 34: 'a stench shall rise up from their corpses.'
Amos 5: 'I have made the stink of your camp to come up into your nostrils.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: 'For beasts of burden to rot in their own dung is for carnal men to end their life in the stench of lust.'
Fourth, as the same Isidore says, by the continual beating of its wings, repeated in the air, it produces a noise, and, as it were, buzzes.
It signifies, according to Proverbs, that men are made worthy of others' rebuke through vanity: 'he that boasts himself, and puffs himself up, stirs up quarrels.'

An example is found in Absalom, 2 Kings 15, and in Haman, Esther 4, and in Adonijah, 1 Kings 1, each of whom was of this kind, and perished in his own folly, Jeremiah 2: 'they have gone after vanity, and are become vain.'
Fifth, as the same Isidore says, with its buzzing and its bite it troubles sleepers, and keeps them from rest.

It signifies the insolence of evil men, restless and troublesome to others. 2 Thessalonians, last chapter: 'we have heard that there are some among you who walk disorderly, working not at all, but curiously meddling. Now these we command and beseech, in the Lord Jesus Christ, that, working with silence, they eat their own bread.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus, Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: Against which, Seneca, to Lucilius: 'the first proof of a well-composed mind is to be able to remain still with itself, and dwell with itself.'
Ecclesiasticus 38: 'hasten to be first in your own house, and there take your ease, and occupy yourself,' and so on.
As the same Isidore says, it flies about especially by night, and pierces and bites the limbs on which it settles.

It signifies hypocrites and false men, who do not walk in the light, and who often greatly harm those close to them, whom they corrupt the more easily. 2 Timothy 2: 'of whom is Philetus and Hymenaeus, who have fallen from the truth, and have overthrown the faith of some.'

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: An example is found in Torquatus, who, as is found in the legend of blessed Tiburtius, betrayed blessed Tiburtius and many other Christians.
It is a lover of light; for it gladly sees the light, and so, less cautiously rushing into a candle or into fire, it is often accustomed, out of its eagerness to see the light, to burn itself.

It signifies the curious, who wish to reach into the mysteries of the Scriptures beyond their own measure, and come to their own peril or destruction. Proverbs 25: 'he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by his glory.'
'The beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, De ecclesiastica hierarchia Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, in the book On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy: 'it is dangerous to wish to unlock secret mysteries to the weak.'
Gnats are of the greatest use for feeding swallows: for gnats, flying about in the air, are reckoned the most welcome prey by swallows, which hunt flies in the air.

They signify that the wicked are prey and refreshment for demons, or that mercenary prelates feed on their poor subjects. Ezekiel 34: 'my flocks became a prey, and my sheep became food for devouring.'

Hence a certain versifier began aptly on such men, and it is found in a certain Gloss on Jeremiah 23, or 34: 'since they do not feed, but are fed upon, they are derived not from "pasco" [I feed], but from "pascor, pasceris" [I am fed, you are fed].'
Against which it is said of David: 'he fed them in the innocence of his heart,' and so on.
The dog-fly is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to our authorities.
For first, as Isidore says, the dog-fly is called a biting fly of the dog kind; and it was of flies of this kind, together with gnats or midges, that the land of Egypt was struck.

They signify the souls of flying and shooting things, from which the holy man is protected by the shield of God's truth and goodness and by the intercession of angels, according to that saying, Psalm 90: 'his truth shall compass you with a shield; you shall not be afraid of the terror of the night, of the arrow that flies in the day,' and so on.
Where, according to the Gloss, four kinds of grave temptations are set forth, from which the holy man who dwells in the help of the Most High is protected.
Jerome: 'human weakness would not be safe amid so many snares of demons, were it not defended by the protection of the holy angels.'

Second, as the same Isidore says, the dog-fly is the worst kind of fly, of large body and broad belly; compared to other flies, weak in flight, but of great tenacity and clinging to the limbs of the animals it settles on. For it buries itself in the fur and hair of animals, especially dogs, and, hiding there, sucks and drinks their blood, so much that it ulcerates and corrodes the flesh, as is clear in the ears of certain dogs, which such flies corrode and ulcerate. Hence it is no wonder: they are foul-smelling, since they are nourished from humors so corrupted and foul.

They signify the beasts of the worst lustful men, clinging tenaciously to the birdlime of lust, and plunging and defiling themselves in it, ulcerating body and soul, and making themselves foul before God and men. 'The beasts of burden have rotted in their own dung.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'for beasts of burden to rot in their own dung is for carnal men to end their life in the stench of lust,' and so on.
The cicada is found, according to the authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as Ambrose says in the Hexameron, the cicada ('cicada') is named from singing ('canendo'), since it forms a wondrous melody with its tiny throat.

It signifies contemplative religious, poor in the Lord, exulting above the level of the mind and marvelously in humility, and inviting others to this very thing. Isaiah 39: 'the meek shall add joy in the Lord, and the poor men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.'
It is sung of blessed Francis that he always devoutly praised God, and invited all creatures to his praise.

Second, as the same Ambrose says, in the midst of burning summer, when the groves are scorched by the noonday heat, then above all it gives forth a clearer song, since at that time it draws in purer air.

It signifies that holy men are especially intent upon, and given to, divine praise and reverence at that time when they, or others, are most afflicted by the tribulations and persecutions of the world, or the devil, or a tyrant. Psalm 76: 'in the day of my trouble I sought God, with my hands lifted up to him in the night, and I was not deceived.'

Of Lawrence, who, set upon the gridiron, with a most beautiful countenance, said: 'I give you thanks, Lord,' and so on, and, smiling, said to Decius: 'learn, wretched man, how great is the power of God; for these coals bring me not burning, but refreshment; but to you, eternal punishment.'

If someone pours oil over the cicada, it is killed at once, since, its pores blocked, it cannot draw in the air it breathes. But if someone at once pours vinegar over it, it revives on the spot, since the force of the vinegar opens the pores that had been blocked by the constriction of the oil. It signifies that flattery — which is signified by the name of oil — does great harm, and frequently kills the soul; but sharp and bitter correction of sins and vices makes the soul cautious, and disposes it to heavenly inspirations, and restores the spiritual life.

And this is what the wise man means, Proverbs 24: 'they that rebuke shall be praised, and blessing shall come upon them. They that say to the wicked man, "you are just," the peoples shall curse them, and the tribes shall abhor them.'
'Better are the wounds of a friend, than the deceitful kisses of an enemy.'

bibl.author: Prosper Aquitanus, Liber sententiarum ex operibus sancti Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, in the Sentences of Prosper: 'the tongues of flatterers bind souls in their sins,' and so on.
The phoenix is proven, according to the saints and others, to have these singular conditions, or properties.

For first, as Isidore says, and Ambrose in the Hexameron, it is said to be a unique bird, and singular in the whole world; hence even laymen marvel at it; hence too, among the Arabs, where the phoenix is born, it is called, that is, named, 'singular.'
'My dove is but one, my perfect one is but one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen of her that bore her. The daughters saw her, and declared her most blessed.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De verbis domini Pseudo Augustini

cit.quote: 'There is one dove that binds, and one that looses.'
Second, as blessed Ambrose says, and the Philosopher too, the phoenix is a bird without equal, living for three hundred, or five hundred, years.

It signifies a singular example of religion, and a persevering longsuffering; it is written in 2 Maccabees 6, of Eleazar, a man advanced in age and of a comely countenance, that, when he was pressed to transgress the law of God, he began to think of the worthy eminence of his age and old age, and the gray hairs of noble birth he had earned, and of his excellent conduct from boyhood, and, according to the statutes of the holy law established by God, answered, saying that he would rather be sent ahead into hell.
Augustine, in the Confessions, of Simplicianus, who, worn down by a long age from his youth, appeared to be a good servant of God, and truly was so.

Third, as the same Ambrose says, blessed Ambrose, and the Philosopher too: when, having completed its three hundred, or five hundred, years, as has been said, it feels the failing of its life, it builds a nest from aromatic and very dry woods, which, in summer, are set alight by the fervor of the sun, the west wind blowing. Once these are kindled, it enters the nest of its own accord, and there, among the already-burning wood, is reduced to ash. From this ash, within three days, a certain little worm is born, which, gradually receiving feathers, is reshaped into a bird.
From the moisture, or ash, of the phoenix, a new little chick arises, and gradually grows up, and, as time passes, puts on the pinions of its wings, and is restored to the appearance of a bird.

It signifies the reformation of a man who is spiritually good, in grace and in glory, or his merits and good works, against death, unto an eternal renewal in the heavens. Ecclesiasticus 14: 'before your death, do good to your friend' — that is, for the sake of Christ, the one true friend, according to the Gloss — 'and, according to your ability, stretching out your hand, give to the poor.'
'Defraud not yourself of the good day, and let not the part of a good gift overpass you.' Psalm: 'who satisfies your desire with good things; your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's.'

Ambrose, in the prayer On the Commendation of the Soul: 'and when the supernal kingdom shall have shone upon all, may you, a new man, joined to the company of all the saints, possess the sweetness of divine contemplation, world without end; may the Son of God establish you within the ever-pleasant, ever-green places of paradise,' and so on.
Fourth, as the same Ambrose and the Philosopher say, it is a most beautiful bird, very like the peacock in its feathers, loving solitude, and seeking its living from clean grains and fruits.

It signifies religious of beautiful form, of gracious and honorable conduct, fleeing worldly things above the level of the mind, and refreshing themselves with the consolation of the Holy Spirit and heavenly grace. James 3: 'the wisdom that is from above, first indeed is chaste, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be persuaded, agreeing to the good, full of mercy and good fruits.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'he to whom God is his portion ought to care for nothing but God. For those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'
It is sung of blessed Dominic: 'keeping the flower of modesty unstained, he attained the celibacy of an exalted life.'

Fifth, as Alan relates, it is a sign of divine acceptance, or an approval, or representation, of a spiritual action. For when Onias, the high priest, had built a temple in Heliopolis, a city of Egypt, in the likeness of the temple of Jerusalem, and, on the first day of Unleavened Bread, had gathered many aromatic woods upon the altar, and had kindled a fire to offer the sacrifice, suddenly, before all who watched, this bird descended into the midst of the pyre, and was at once burned up in the fire of the sacrifice, and reduced to ash. But the ash remaining, and being carefully kept by the priest's command, within three days a certain little worm was created from that ash, which, finally taking the form of a bird, flew away into solitude.

It signifies not so much the divine or heavenly acceptance of spiritual sacrifices, as the death of Christ, suffering on the cross, and his resurrection within three days, and his flying away, or ascension, into heaven: 'it behooved Christ to suffer, and to rise again from the dead, and so to enter into his glory.'
Ambrose, on Paul's letter to the Hebrews: 'Christ suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven, exalted to the right hand of the Father.'
The crane is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.
For first, as Ambrose says in the Hexameron, it is a bird of great wings and strong flight, seeking the heights of the air so as to see to what regions it wishes to travel.

It signifies Paul, powerful prelates, or contemplatives no less great and eminent, such as he who was caught up to the third heaven and into paradise, where he heard secret words which it is not granted to man to utter.

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: Absorbed into God, and now made, as it were, a fellow-citizen of the angels.

A bird greatly loving its own kind, fond of company, and flying in orderly formation. Its leader, moreover, as though rebuking and correcting, drives the flock by voice to fly straight, and if it should perhaps grow hoarse, another crane succeeds it.

It signifies charity and the ordered life of religious, or of others living commonly in society and under correction, Acts 4: 'the multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul; neither did any one say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them.'
'I rejoice, though absent in body, present in spirit, seeing your good order.'
Song of Songs 2: 'he set charity in order in me.'
Augustine, in the Confessions: 'Milan was full of good brothers, under Ambrose, the nourishing bishop of piety.'

Aristotle, in the book of Animals, and blessed Ambrose: cranes make for the ground with a herald's cry, and once they have settled, they set watches over themselves, so that the others may rest more securely. The watchers stand straight on one leg, and hold a small stone in the other foot, raised or lifted from the ground, so that, should they by chance fall asleep, they may be roused by the falling of the stone.

They signify the watchfulness, care, and circumspection which the prelates of churches ought to have, and how much, concerning those entrusted to them, Acts 20: 'take heed to yourselves, and to the whole flock, wherein the Holy Spirit has placed you bishops, to rule the Church which he has purchased with his own blood.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, On Consideration, to Pope Eugenius: pastors ought to show themselves such that they 'are upright in judgment, provident in counsel, discreet in commanding, diligent in arranging, strenuous in acting, not idle in leisure.'
Fourth, as the same Aristotle says, cranes are ash-colored in their youth, but in old age, the longer they live, the blacker they become.

They signify that, in those who wish to be saved, penance, and humility, and self-abasement ought to increase at every age. Lamentations 3: 'it is good for a man, when he has borne the yoke from his youth.'
Bernard and Gregory, in various sayings: 'on the way of God, not to advance is to fall back.'
Fifth, as the same Aristotle says, if any of them stray from the company, the others, crying out, seek and call back their lost companions.

They signify preachers who, by their teaching and exhortation, call back their neighbors straying from the way of truth, and lead them back to the way of salvation, and restore them to the unity and the bosom of mother Church. James, last chapter: 'my brothers, if any of you err from the truth, and one convert him, he must know that he who causes a sinner to be converted from the error of his way shall save his soul from death, and shall cover a multitude of sins.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: 'Nothing so pleases God as zeal for the saving of souls.'
Sixth, as the same Aristotle says, when they see a heron or a hawk coming above them, they raise their beaks upward and, as best they can, defend themselves with the sharpness of their beaks.

They signify that good men cannot better defend themselves from the attack of demons than by lifting the mind to God, or by holy prayer and the confession of sins. Matthew: 'watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation.'
The Gloss on Nehemiah, chapter 8: 'prayer is the one refuge against plagues.'
The cock is found, according to our authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.

For first, as Isidore says, the cock ('gallus') is named from castration ('castratio'). For, among all other birds, this one alone has its testicles removed; for the ancients called castrated males 'galli.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Commentarii Hieronymi in prophetas minores

cit.quote: And Jerome's Gloss on Hosea 4 says this very thing: 'it signifies prelates, who especially ought to be most chaste.' Proverbs 30: 'a cock with his loins girded, and a ram; and there is no king that can resist him.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: 'Linen breeches were prescribed for priests, to be worn at the loins, since the chastity of the Gospel is commanded to the ministers and rulers of the churches.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Second, as Pliny says, in book 29, chapter 4: 'raw cock's flesh, applied to a serpent's bite, removes the venom; and its brain, taken in a drink, is effective for the same purpose. If anyone is also anointed with its fat, or the yolk of its egg, he will be safe from panthers and lions. If, too, the bones of cocks or hens are mixed into molten gold, they consume it entirely; hence hen bone is a poison to gold.'

They signify that evangelical continence is of great benefit, in any man whatever, for many things, and is especially, in spiritual ways, manifold in its power as a remedy. Judith 15: 'your heart has been strengthened in the Lord your God, and you have acted with courage, because you have loved chastity, and have known no other man after your husband.'
Ambrose: 'let us, then, resist the manifold evils of this age with chastity and chaste deeds.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily On a Simple Confessor: 'no good work is worth anything without chastity, nor is chastity worth anything without good work.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: ...its hens, boldly attacking their adversaries with beak and spurs.
It signifies both the sheep, and the boldness of prelates and preachers, for their churches and the souls entrusted to them. John 10: 'the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: 'Nothing so pleases God as zeal for souls.'

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fourth, as the same author puts it, in the same place, once victory has been gained over its adversaries, it at once sings.

It signifies that good men, triumphing over hostile assaults, or vices, ought to give thanks to God, following the example of Moses, Exodus 15, who, after his victory over the Egyptians, sang a song to the Lord with the children of Israel.
The ancient fathers in the desert of Egypt did similar things in similar circumstances, as Jerome relates in the Lives of the Fathers.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Fifth, as the same Pliny says, in the same place, before it crows, it beats itself with its wings, and, striking itself, makes itself fitter for crowing.

It signifies the preacher of the Gospel who, so as to preach well and fruitfully to others, first chastises himself, and amends his own life, following the example of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 9: 'I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: 'Let not your deeds confound your words, lest, when you speak in church, someone silently say to himself, "physician, heal yourself."'
As Ambrose says, in the deeper hours of the night it is accustomed to give forth its song clearer and stronger, but around the morning hour it forms a lighter voice.

It signifies preachers of the Gospel who, in times of the Church's more severe tribulations or persecutions, preach most vigorously, offer comfort, and cry out to God; and when these cease, or nearly so, they nonetheless, as is fitting, do not entirely cease from these same things, in their own way, following the example of the Apostle Paul, Colossians 1: 'we cease not to pray and to beg for you,' and so on.
'Besides those things that are without, there is my daily concern, the care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'for Paul was often torn apart, bitten, afflicted, when he saw some perishing. And he hastened to gather all into the kingdom of God.'
It wears a red crest on its head like a crown, and once this is lost, it at once loses its boldness, and grows, as it were, older toward attacking its adversary.
It signifies that a man who is a prelate, or a preacher, or another who has charity, or heavenly wisdom, at the summit of his soul, can prevail against any adversaries whatsoever.

But he who lacks this cannot, and rather must succumb, following the example of Peter, who, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, was of such great fear that, at the voice of a single serving-maid, fearing to die, he denied his life, as Gregory says, and as is found in Mark 14.

But after the coming of the Holy Spirit, namely in the assembly of the rulers and elders, before all the people, he said steadfastly, Acts 4: 'we ought to obey God rather than men. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.'

Blessed Gregory also gives an example, in book 3 of the Dialogues, of a certain bishop who, in Greece, with his tongue cut out, preached most brilliantly, and with the greatest fervor, against the adversaries of the faith, in Greece, together with two other, more holy bishops. This one, however, having fallen into fornication, immediately lost the gift of his tongue.

Eighth, as the same [Ambrose] says: it loves its hens, and, when it finds food, calls them with a certain voice, and withdraws from it itself, so as to refresh and feed them; it keeps the more tender and plump one, which it loves more, nearer to itself, for the sake of quiet, and desires her presence around itself the more. In the morning, when it has flown out to pasture, it applies its side first to hers, and, by certain nods, entices and invites her to mate with it, and fights specially for her, as though jealous, and drives off approaching cocks from itself with beak and spurs, and, attacking, strikes the ground with its beak, and raises the feathers around its neck, so as to show itself bold; it also raises the feathers of its tail, as much as it can, upward, so as to gird itself for battle. These things signify the love that a prelate ought to have for his subjects, and how he ought to prefer the better, more worthy, or more useful among them to the others, and keep them near himself. Likewise, that if he wishes to fight for his subjects against adversaries, he ought to have contempt for earthly things and desire for eternal ones. For to strike the ground with the beak is to despise temporal things out of zeal.

But to raise the feathers of the tail upward is to direct one's desires upward, in perseverance. Ecclesiasticus 10: 'their ruler is in the midst of the brothers, in honor; and they that fear God shall be in his eyes.'
'We became, in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishing her children.'
'Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanities and false follies.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, On Consideration, to Eugenius: let shepherds be such as, indeed, to 'show themselves as John to kings, Moses to the Egyptians, Phinehas to fornicators, Elijah to idolaters, Elisha to the greedy, Peter to liars, Paul to blasphemers, Christ to the money-changers; who are vigorous in acting, diligent in disposing.'
...the lion fears and shudders at it, especially if it is white.
For the lion dreads the white cock, as Pliny says.
It signifies that the devil, and the powerful of this world, fear good men, and especially prelates and teachers, in whom Christ and the chastity of the Gospel dwell.
We have an example in Paul, Acts 19, whose garments — indeed, even the small aprons and handkerchiefs carried away from his body — drove demons out of the possessed, and healed every infirmity.
Chrysostom: 'do you wish to know the gifts of God? The garments of Paul were a terror to demons.'

...of Pharaoh, and of his servants; and likewise of Elijah, how he was feared by Ahab and Jezebel, 1 Kings 17 and after; and by Ahaziah and his companies of fifty, 2 Kings 1; and likewise of John the Baptist, how he was feared by Herod, Mark 6.
Tenth, as Pliny says, seeking its living with beak and feet, it turns over and scratches through the chaff, and, once it has found grain, calls out to the hens, and summons them.

bibl.author: Epistola Pauli ad Timotheum prima, Apostolus

cit.quote: It signifies the labor of good prelates and teachers, and their diligence concerning works of piety, following the pattern of the Apostle, 1 Timothy 4: 'exercise yourself unto piety.'
Ambrose, in the Ordinary Gloss, there: 'the sum of the Christian religion consists in piety, and he who has it will obtain mercy in the end.'

Eleventh, as the same Pliny says, the cock fears the eagle and the hawk, plunderers of the land, since such birds of prey lie in wait for birds walking about on the ground. And so, since the cock has very keen sight, it keeps one eye lowered to seek its food, and directs the other upward into the air, to guard against the coming of the eagle or the hawk. As soon as it sees one or the other coming from a distance, it at once calls out to the hens, and, fleeing, hides itself in houses, or crags, or hedges.

It signifies that good prelates and teachers hold demons and their temptations in suspicion, and dread and fear them, and are watchful and circumspect against their cunning, both for themselves and for other faithful members of their household. Luke 21: 'watch, therefore, praying at all times, that you may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that are to come, and to stand before the Son of Man.'
'Be sober, and watch, because your adversary the devil,' and so on.

bibl.author: Iohannes Damascenus, De fide orthodoxa Iohannis Damasceni

cit.quote: Damascene, in his little book: 'every malice and every uncleanness were devised by the devil.'

bibl.author: Beda Venerabilis, Expositio Bede in Marci Evangelium

cit.quote: The cock lays eggs in its last and decrepit old age, and produces certain small eggs, very round, and, as it were, livid or saffron-colored, from which, if warmed by some venomous worm during the dog-days, a basilisk is created.

It signifies sinners grown old in evil, cherished by the devil in their malice in a time of worldly prosperity, who are the cause of the future coming of the Antichrist, or of some other very great danger — and especially those great sinners who ought to build up others, and instead corrupt them by their evil examples. Lamentations 4: 'the kings of the earth, and all the inhabitants of the world, would not have believed that the adversary and the enemy should enter in by the gates of Jerusalem: because of the sins of her prophets, and the iniquities of her priests, who shed the blood of the just in the midst of her.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, De viris illustribus Hieronymi

cit.quote: Jerome, in the book On Illustrious Men: 'Josephus relates, in his History, that Jerusalem was overwhelmed on account of the murder of James the Just.'

...the cock, its inner parts thrown away, filled with the seed of garden saffron and with polypody, and cooked with five pounds of water until the water is nearly consumed, becomes most beneficial for those suffering from choleric passion; it purges viscous and phlegmatic humors, helps those suffering from melancholy, expels great flatulence of the stomach, eases pain, and cures the swelling and pain of the arteries; it is also effective against the prolonged length of an intermittent fever.

It signifies that the examples of worthy elders dissolve every kind of spiritual infirmity in the hearts of their subjects, or of lesser men. We have an example in the ancient fathers, the patriarchs, the prophets, and the apostles.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Likewise, in those fifteen hundred fathers, of whom Ambrose writes in the book On Paradise.
Likewise, in the five thousand monks dwelling in various cells, as Jerome writes in letter 46.
'Stand upon the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, which is the good way, and walk in it, and you shall find refreshment for your souls.'
James, last chapter: 'take, my brothers, for an example of longsuffering and patience, the prophets who spoke to you,' and so on.
The capon is found to have these conditions, or properties.

...the cock, which is so called because of the removal of its testicles, and, in the manner of other animals, is entirely changed in its temperament. For it loses its crest, lays aside its boldness, loses its crowing, does not distinguish the hours of the night, does not beat itself with its wings, nor gird itself for battle.

It signifies a prelate who, because of his sins and notable failings, in both life and knowledge, of remissness and negligence, has lost the power to beget spiritual children for God, and virtues, and grace, and good repute — of whom it is rightly said, Isaiah 22, that he is to be removed from the Church: 'behold,' he says, 'the Lord will cause you to be carried away, as a capon is carried away,' and so on.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Epistola Hieronymi ad Heliodorum monachum

cit.quote: Jerome, in the exhortatory letter to Heliodorus the bishop, near the end: 'you are a delicate brother, if you wish to rejoice in this world, and after death to reign with Christ.'

Likewise, in the same place: 'it is not easy to hold the rank of the blessed Peter and Paul, already reigning with Christ, lest perhaps the angel of the Lord come down from heaven with his sword drawn, and kill them, and move their lampstand from its place.'

Second, as the same author says, it broods over eggs not its own, as if it were a hen, taking on the office of a female, and nourishes and leads about the young of others; it even imitates the hen's voice, calling the chicks with a hoarse cackling, joining itself to the hens and devouring their food with them; but it does not refresh them, nor does it fight for them or against them, nor does it fatten them, nor is it fattened by them.

It signifies carnal, base, and effeminate prelates, doing no works of virtue in the Church, rejoicing only in the name of their office, keeping company with the weak and the friendships of women — which is one of God's angers, or curses, upon a sinful people. Isaiah 3: 'I will give children to be their princes, and the effeminate shall rule over them.'
'They kept company with harlots, and sacrificed with effeminate men.'
The chapter, which is blessed Ambrose's: 'he who is more excellent in honor is to be reckoned most base, unless he excels in holiness.'
Third, as the same author says, the capon is of a slower spirit than the cock, and of moister and softer flesh, and greater fat, and looser plumage.

It signifies hypocrites and evil men, pretending a greater maturity, piety, gentleness, and devotion than the rest, and yet it is not so, since others are better than they. Titus 1: 'they profess that they know God, but in their works they deny him, being abominable, and unbelieving, and to every good work reprobate.'
'Having an appearance of piety, but denying its power.'
'Pretenders and cunning men provoke the wrath of God.'

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: An example is found in Torquatus, of whom mention is made in the legend of blessed Tiburtius.

Fourth, as Constantine says, the flesh of a castrated cock of this kind is more suitable than the flesh of any other fowl; for it produces more praiseworthy nourishment and better blood. Its brains, too, are more beneficial than the brains of other birds.

It signifies that a true guardian, in soul and body, is incomparable to other men, and produces more praiseworthy and useful fruit and edification in the Church. Ecclesiasticus 26: 'no weight is worthy of a continent soul.'
An example is found in the apostles, and in the blessed virgins — the glorious mother of Christ, Agnes, Agatha, Catherine, and Lucy, and so on.
The hen is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.
A bird of great endurance and of much brooding, or egg-laying.
They signify sons and preachers who beget many children for the Gospel: 'in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I have begotten you.'
Ambrose, in the sermon On a Bishop Confessor: 'how great is the joy that comes of the wisdom and devotion of these his sons.'

Second, as Aristotle says, many hens lay eggs without coupling, and eggs of this kind are called wind-eggs, and are more tasteless and less praiseworthy than other eggs. Some hens, too, always produce twins, and one of the two is small and sometimes deformed.

They signify those who preach for vainglory, and for vanity, whose adulterated words do not produce for God children who are chosen and well-formed, praiseworthy or acceptable to God, but for the most part deformed and vain ones, 2 Corinthians 2: 'we are not as many, adulterating the word of God, but with sincerity, as from God, before God, in Christ, we speak.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that, lamenting, he used to say of such preachers, and preferred to them, in merit and fruit of edification, the simple brothers of holy conversation, proving it by 1 Kings 2: the barren one — that is, the simple brother who holds no office in the Church — has borne many children for God, and she that had many children has grown weak.

Aristotle, in the book of Animals: hens brood over their eggs for three days, and at once the signs of the chick appear, and this happens in the larger eggs over more days, and in the smaller ones after fewer, and the chick is generated from the white and nourished from the yolk.

They signify the varied effect of preaching, according to more and less, whose progress arises and is known in chastity and mercy or charity or piety or heavenly devotion, 2 Corinthians 2: 'for to this end I also wrote, that I may know the experiment of you, whether you be obedient in all things. And to whom you have pardoned anything, I also; for what I have pardoned, if I have pardoned anything, for your sakes have I done it in the person of Christ.'

Whence a certain holy father used to say, as is set down in the Lives of the Fathers by blessed Jerome, that whoever wishes to know the progress of his own salvation ought to look to the increase of humility and of the other virtues.
As Aristotle says, in book 4, hens that lay too much are not long-lived, but die quickly.

They signify men greatly increasing in children and in the riches or prosperities of this world, who cannot long endure, God not permitting it, and, because of their ingratitude, the whole assembly of the saints complaining of them, Job 21: 'why then do the wicked live, are they advanced, and strengthened with riches? Their seed continues before them, a multitude of kinsmen, and of children's children, in their sight. They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell.'
'He that strives to do many things shall fall into judgment.'
'My son, let not your acts be in many things, for if you meddle with many, you shall not be blameless in one.'

Jerome, in the letter On the Twelve Luminaries: 'Paulinus seemed a teacher to his son, and had not before been a pupil; he attempted to arise and become fruitful without a root. And so his writings need no scribe, and no paper.'

Fifth, as the Gloss on Matthew 23 touches on, it is a bird of piety toward its chicks. For it warms its chicks under its wings against the kite, grows sick at their sorrow and loses its feathers, feeds and satisfies its chicks more than itself; and, once it has found food, it gathers and calls them, and, lest they be seized by a hawk or a kite, protects and defends them under the covering of its wings, as has been touched on, and shows its affection for its chicks by the roughness of its feathers and the hoarseness of its voice.

All these things signify the solicitude, diligence, and compassion that a shepherd ought to have for his subjects; likewise the preacher, for his converts. Galatians 4: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'
'Most gladly will I spend, and be spent myself, for your souls.'

Against which, on the part of the subjects, or hearers, who are like the hen, but who do not accept her: Matthew 23: 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'as though Paul had given birth to the whole world, so did he hasten to bring all into the kingdom of God.'
Griffins have these properties, or conditions, according to our authorities.

For Deuteronomy 14 counts it among flying things; and, as the Gloss says there: 'it is four-footed, similar in head and wings to an eagle, resembling a lion in the rest of its body; it dwells in the Hyperborean mountains, and is especially hostile to horses and to men.'

In its nest it places an emerald stone, against the beasts of the mountain. Concerning this creature, since it will be treated more fully in the treatise On Animals, under the letter G, since it is, in part, classed among the animals, I have not thought it should be set down further here.
For indeed you will find the moral applications concerning these same points, and many others, treated there in their proper order.

bibl.author: Glossa super Psalmos, Glossa super Psalmos

cit.quote: The heron, which is also commonly called the falcon, but is properly named the coot, as is found in the Gloss on the Psalms — 'the house of the heron,' or 'the house of the coot,' according to the letter used by the Church — has these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.
For first, as Gregory says, it is a royal bird, greedy for prey, accustomed to being carried on the hand.

It signifies men familiar with the Holy Spirit, always eager and diligent for fresh heavenly refreshments, or consolations. Psalm 72: 'I am always with you; you have held me by my right hand, and by your will you have conducted me, and with your glory you have received me. For what have I in heaven? And besides you what do I desire upon earth? My flesh and my heart has fainted away; you are the God of my heart, and the God that is my portion forever.'
The Gloss, on the beginning of Romans: 'to serve God is to reign.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Divine consolation is a delicate thing, and is not given to those who possess what belongs to another.'
Augustine: 'charity is a spring of its own, in which a stranger has no share.'

Second, as the same Gregory says, it is a bold bird, in the manner of the hawk, having little flesh in proportion to its body, but much plumage, and so its flight is very light, since there is little in it that weighs it down, and much that raises and lifts it.
It signifies the poor in spirit, freed from carnal things and enriched with virtues, and so most swiftly driving themselves upward toward God. 'The poor men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.'
2 Corinthians 8: 'their deep poverty has abounded unto the riches of their simplicity.'
Blessed Vincent, Christ's poor man, set upon the rack, said, as is read in his passion: 'I am carried up on high, and, set higher, I despise these lowest things of the world.'
Bernard, in his sermons: 'many see our crosses, who do not see our anointings.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Third, as the same Gregory says, in the Moralia: it is of great boldness, of a most sharp breast, and a strong talon, and it harms its prey more by striking it with its breast than with its talon. But if it does not seize its prey on the first or second attempt, it seeks, as it were, vengeance on itself. Hence, if it is a wild one, it scarcely hunts prey for the rest of that day; but if it is a tame one, as though out of shame, it wanders through the air, and does not readily return then to the hand that carries it, since it considers itself defeated and degenerate, when it does not triumph over the bird it has attacked.

It signifies the boldness, or magnanimity, and strength of prelates, rooted in charity and in the recognition of divine goodness and their own frailty. 2 Corinthians 2: 'now thanks be to God, who always makes us triumph in Christ Jesus, and manifests the odor of his knowledge by us in every place.'
'Wherein any man dares — I speak foolishly — I dare also,' and so on.

'Paul feared no dangers, blushed at no mockeries, but, with his will inflamed and his flesh mortified, did all things, and, as though he owed God recompense for time already spent, so did he conduct all his affairs; so did he gather spiritual gain from every side. For, as though always girded for battle, and plotting a certain fire of war, so was he bold. He reckoned the raging fury of tyrants to be, as it were, mere gnats.' Thus far Chrysostom.

As blessed Ambrose says in the Hexameron: the heron, or falcon, is a bird that, among all the birds of prey, has a pious disposition and spirit toward chicks in general. 'With the same diligent service,' he says, 'by which it feeds its own offspring, it likewise nourishes a chick cast off, or unrecognized, by an eagle.'
