Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it nests in hay and feathers, and keeps its nest clean of dung, casting the droppings of its chicks out of the nest, and compelling them to cast it out too.
It signifies those who despise temporal things, and serve God in poverty, keeping cleanness, and procuring that others keep it too.
'I count all things but loss for the sake of Jesus Christ my Lord, for whom I have counted all things as loss, and I esteem them as dung, that I may gain Christ.'
'I would,' he says, 'that all men were even as myself.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on 'this is my commandment': 'behold,' he says, 'the elect of God tame the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command the demons, shine with virtues, despise present things, preach the eternal homeland by their voices and their conduct, love it even in dying, and reach it through torments; they can be killed, but cannot be bent.'
Sixth, as the same Isidore says, it feeds its chicks with spiders, worms, and flies.

It signifies base men, who take their pasture from vile, withered, vain, and passing things, and set their life and hope in the superficial, fleeting, and pleasant delights of this life. Hosea 12: 'Ephraim feeds on wind, and follows the burning heat; all the day long he multiplies lying and desolation; he made a covenant with the Assyrians, and carried oil into Egypt.'
Proverbs 10: 'he that trusts to lies, feeds the winds; and the same runs after birds that fly away.'
An example is found in all who set up Haman, Esther 4, and Adonijah, 1 Kings 1, and Absalom, 2 Kings 15, and many others, like Julian the Apostate, and so on.
It eats the poison of henbane without stumbling or harm.

It signifies those who, as though in a state of despair, commit themselves to every danger for the filling of the body, or for the fulfillment of their own intent, of whom the Lord complains, Isaiah 65: 'I have spread forth my hands all the day to an unbelieving people, that walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts. A people that continually provokes me to anger before my face.'

An example is found in two sons of an emperor who, as Jerome puts it in the Lives of the Fathers, stretched nets for hunting in the desert for forty miles, and cornered a certain holy old man, around whom, venting their fury out of ill will, they tried to force him to deny Christ; but they heard from him that they would die the following day by God's judgment, and so it happened.
Eighth, as the same Isidore says, it sometimes suffers and contracts leprosy and the falling sickness.
Mark 9: 'often it cast him into the fire, and into water, to destroy him.'
Such cases are cured only by prayer and fasting, as is found in the same place.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'what is more distant than to withdraw from oneself, and to have, through the intervening heat of worldly lust, a divorce from the saints?'
Ninth, as Aristotle says, the female lives longer than the male.
It signifies certain effeminate and evil men prospering longer, according to the age, than virtuous and good men.
Ecclesiastes 7: 'the just man perishes in his justice, and the wicked man lives a long time in his malice.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Enarrationes in Psalmos Augustini

cit.quote: But in such cases one must attend to the words of blessed Augustine: 'every wicked man,' he says, 'either lives so that he may be corrected, or so that a good man may be exercised through him.'
The male is jealous for his mate, and is accustomed to fight for her.

It signifies that everyone ought to be jealous, in the higher part of reason, for the lower, lest it be invaded by the enemy. Likewise, that every prelate ought to be jealous for his church, and for every soul entrusted to him, for every advancement in grace, and for its preservation in freedom, truth, and justice.
'Strive for justice for your soul, and contend even unto death for justice, and God will fight your enemies for you.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Morlanensis, De contemptu mundi Bernardi Morlanensis

cit.quote: 'It is not fitting for the handmaid to rule, and the mistress to serve.' And this speaks of the lower and higher part of reason, of which the higher ought to rule universally in the kingdom of the soul, for the preservation of all goodness, holiness, and justice.
Eleventh, as the same Aristotle says, it fears and hates the weasel, and, by crying out and calling loudly, betrays its presence.

It signifies that the devil is to be feared, that is, held in suspicion, hated, and abhorred, and, once his temptation is perceived, that one must cry out to God, and the saints, and the angels, in prayer.
'In the day of my trouble I cried to you, since you heard me.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily for Quinquagesima Sunday: 'the stronger the tumult of carnal thoughts that presses upon us, the more fervently we ought to cry out in prayer.'
The Gloss on Nehemiah, chapter 8: 'prayer is the one refuge against enemies.'
As the author says, to occupy the nests of swallows, it opposes them with beak and bites.

It signifies plunderers, or those who overstep and defraud their brothers; against which, 1 Thessalonians 4: 'that no man overreach, nor circumvent his brother in business, because the Lord is the avenger of all such things, as we have told you before, and testified.'
Laban, Genesis 30 and 31, who so many times deceived the faithful Jacob.
'Sparrows, their chicks, mothers, fathers.'
It signifies pious and charitable men, toward widows, orphans and wards, pilgrims and strangers, the afflicted and the destitute.

Job 29: 'the blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow. I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame. I was the father of the poor. The stranger did not lodge outside, my door was open to the traveler.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: Piety, which, according to the Apostle, is profitable to all things, had filled the heart of Francis with abundant fullness; it drove him upward, through devotion, into God; it transformed him, through compassion, into Christ; it inclined him, through condescension, toward his neighbor; it refigured him, through reconciliation with the other creatures, back to the state of innocence.
A crowd of sparrows call one another mutually, and, to free one that has been captured, hasten and rush as best they can.
It signifies how much diligence and charity one man ought to have for another, in a time of adversity and danger.
Proverbs 6: 'run about, hasten, stir up your friend.'
'Deliver them that are led to death, and cease not to deliver them that are drawn to destruction.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De diversis questionibus octoginta tribus

cit.quote: Augustine, book 83 of Questions: 'nothing so proves a friend as bearing a friend's burden.'

An example is found in two philosopher friends, of whom blessed Ambrose writes in the book On Holy Virginity, that when one of them had been condemned, and, on the sabbath day of his beheading, was without doubt awaiting and desiring to arrange matters concerning his house and his children in person, the other willingly entered prison to die in his place, if he did not return. But since he faithfully returned, while his substitute was being led to execution, it happened that the great faith and friendship of both was reported at once to the emperor, who was nearby in his palace; he at once absolved the condemned man, and set both of them as friends at his side, saying that it befitted an emperor to have such friends.

An example is found likewise in blessed Paulinus, bishop of Nola, who gave himself up in place of a widow's son, as blessed Gregory relates in book 3 of the Dialogues, chapter 1, and consequently led back all the other captives too.
The ostrich is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to the authorities.
For first, as Isidore says, it took its name from a Greek word, since it has the body of an animal, yet has feathers as a bird does, and two feet, and a beak like a bird.

...hypocrites, who are carnal and wish to seem spiritual, seeking heavenly things by outward show of contemplation and devotion, Titus 1: 'they profess that they know God, but in their works they deny him, being abominable, and incredulous.'
'Having an appearance indeed of godliness, but denying the power thereof.'

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: Such were Muhammad, as is found in his deeds, and Nicholas, the newcomer from Antioch, as is found in his errors, and Torquatus, as is found in the Passion of blessed Tiburtius, who, under the cloak of virtue, advanced the cause of falsehood.
Second, as the same Isidore states, because of the heaviness of its body, it is not lifted into the air along with other birds.

It signifies those who love, or follow, carnal indulgences and bodily rest, and cannot rise with spiritual men to divine things, Proverbs 20: 'wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness riotous; whosoever is delighted therewith shall not be wise.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, On the Spirit and the Soul: 'bodily delight hinders the knowledge of spiritual good'; against which, Ecclesiastes 2: 'I thought in my heart to withdraw my flesh from wine, that I might turn my mind to wisdom, and might avoid folly.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: It is sung of blessed Martin, a man of sober life, as is found in his Life, that, 'his eyes and hands always intent upon heaven, he never relaxed his unconquered spirit from prayer.'

Likewise it is read of blessed Francis, his senses wholly mortified, that he was suspended wholly in God, even lifted bodily from the earth, a heavenly brightness surrounding him and the place where he prayed, in a marvelous manner, seen at night by his companions in the wilderness.
Third, as the same Isidore states, it lays eggs like a bird, but neglects to warm them; yet, cast into the sand, they are quickened by the warmth of the dust.
It signifies negligent prelates: 'like the ostrich, she leaves her eggs on the earth, and forgets that the foot may tread upon them, or that the beasts of the field may crush them.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: 'She is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers'; against which blessed Martin used to say, as is found in his Life: 'Lord, if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor on their account.'
The Apostle says something similar, Philippians 1.
Fourth, as Aristotle says, it is of such heat that it swallows and consumes iron.

It signifies those in the Church, or a congregation, who have an immoderate zeal, so much so that sometimes it even casts down the strong, and leads to spiritual change and consumption. Romans 10: 'I bear them witness that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Let charity inflame the zealous man, knowledge inform him, constancy make him firm. Let him be fervent, let him be circumspect, let him be unconquered. Lest you be seduced by the spirit of lying, let Christ, the truth, shine for you; lest you be led away by the glory of the world or by pleasures, let the wisdom of Christ be sweet to you; lest you be wearied by adversities, let Christ, the power of God, strengthen you.'

Fifth, as Avicenna says, since it is a bird of good size, it lays very large eggs with very hard shells, so that, while occupied in generating them, the heat may be tempered, and excessive heat not be the cause of their dying too quickly.

It signifies the great hope of eternal glory, in the present life, which, together with sobriety of life and zeal, advances holy men, out of charity, toward the bringing forth of holy works. Titus 3: 'looking for the blessed hope, and coming of the glory of the great God and our savior Jesus Christ; let us live soberly, and justly, and godly, in this world.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia, and elsewhere: 'the holy men of God lead their life in patience, but their death in desire.'

Blessed Jerome relates an example, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, of a certain holy father who laughed three times as he was dying, since those attending him feared death, while he himself went joyfully to his rest.
Sixth, as the same author says, it has many feathers in the lower part of its body.

It signifies those abounding in delights and pleasures, as regards sense, and especially generation, whose voice is, as in Wisdom: 'come, let us enjoy the good things that are present. Let us crown ourselves with roses. Let no meadow be free from our luxury. For this is our portion, and this our lot.'
Such men can in no way savor divine things, being wholly bent toward earthly ones.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities never deserve to know divine things.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: As Gregory says, on Job: its feather is like the feathers of the heron and the hawk in color, but not in power. 'For it has the likeness of a feather, but lacks the swiftness of flight'; it raises its wings for flight, but is nonetheless in no way lifted from the earth into the air; 'it is clothed with sparse feathers, and is weighed down in its great body.'
It signifies those who make a show of the appearance of a pig, or a sow: 'a beautiful and foolish woman.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore, De meditatione Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: 'The reason why so few advance is this: that all have their eye turned outward, toward the appearance of the work, and not inward, toward the profit of virtue.'
'Favor is deceitful, and beauty is vain,' and so on. Last chapter of Proverbs.

Eighth, as the same Gregory says, when the time comes for it to lay eggs, it lifts its eyes to the Pleiades; for it lays no eggs except when that constellation rises or ascends. But when it sees those stars, around the month of June, it lays then.

It signifies holy men who, in all the good things they do, always hold and lift their intentions, vows, and affections toward heaven. Colossians 3: 'all whatsoever you do, in word or in work, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks always to God the Father.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore, De virtute orandi Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: 'God is in no way better inclined to hear us than when the mind turns to him with the whole affection of devotion.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: An example is found in blessed Martin who, as is found in his Life, 'with eyes and hands always intent on heaven, did not relax his unconquered spirit from prayer.'
Ninth, as the same Gregory says, once it has laid its eggs, it hides them in the sand, and covers them, and forgets, and so never returns to them.

It signifies those who beget spiritual sons or daughters in the Church, and afterward take no care for their advancement or state; against which: 'my little children, of whom I am in labor again, until Christ be formed in you.'
'We became, in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishing her children.'
An example is found in blessed John the Evangelist, as is found in his Life and Acts, of how he cherished those he converted, especially the young robber he had converted.
'Chicks.'
It signifies those who recognize and cherish their own, or even others, in prosperity, but not in adversity, according to that saying, Psalm 48: 'he will praise you when you shall do well to him.'
The Gloss, there: 'praise that comes from prosperity is suspect.'
Ecclesiasticus 12: 'a friend shall not be known in prosperity, and an enemy shall not be hidden in adversity.'

Eleventh, as the author says, it naturally hates the horse, and is so opposed to it that the horse cannot see it without terror. And if the horse should meet it, it raises its wings as against an enemy, and, with the beating of its wings, forces it, as it were, to flee.

It signifies that the wicked rise up against the good, and cannot bear to see them, and, with all the presumption they can muster, lead them to confusion. 2 Timothy 3: 'now as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith. But they shall proceed no further; for their folly shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was.'

Chrysostom, in the sermon for the third Sunday in Lent: 'the wicked cannot bear to see what is good. The wicked do not wish the better man to live, lest they, degenerate, should have to bear reproaches for their own baseness; so the life of the good is a torment to the very worst.'

div.head: Cap. 36: De papagallo seu de psittaco

cit.quote: The parrot is a bird of which blessed Ambrose writes, in the Hexameron, book 5, chapters 17 and 26, that it is a bird having a voice clearly formed in the manner of a man's. For he says thus: 'from where do I get the voices of a parrot?'; and again: 'how clearly formed is the parrot's voice!'

It signifies, by this bird, with its green color known to all and its red beak, the evangelical preachers, faithfully shining forth in the catholic faith, speaking with the fervor of the Holy Spirit, and clearly pronouncing the words of God to all, according to Habakkuk 2: 'the just man lives by his faith.'
Ecclesiasticus 48: 'his word burned like a torch.'
And in Psalm 18: 'their sound has gone forth into all the earth,' and so on.

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita, Epistole Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, in the letter to Timothy on the death of Peter and Paul, calls Paul the loud-sounding trumpet of all the churches.
The turtledove has these properties, or meanings, according to the authorities.
For first, as Isidore says, it is so named from its mournful and groaning voice.

It signifies holy or religious men, always groaning and sighing for eternal things. Romans 8: 'ourselves also, having the first-fruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of the sons of God.'
It is written of blessed [Dominic] that he made of his eyes, as it were, a fountain of tears, and those tears were his bread day and night.
It is also written of blessed Francis that he found no consolation except in tears, on account of which he lost his eyesight before his time.
Second, as the same Isidore says, it is, like the dove, simple, but far less cheerful.

It signifies certain simple men in the Church, or religious, little children in the malice of gall, but refreshed with the sweetness of charity and love, and of heavenly consolation. 1 Corinthians 14: 'do not become children in sense, but in malice be children; but in sense be perfect.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: For this reason Ambrose says, on Luke, that 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot savor divine things.'

It is called a chaste bird, from its character, or its movements, since it is a companion of chastity; for, once it has lost its mate, it seeks no other union, walks and chooses solitary places, and, mindful of its former companionship, always groans, and greatly flees the company of men.

It signifies, for religious men, true lovers of chastity, driving themselves upward toward heavenly things alone, once earthly company is lost, worldly vanities renounced. 2 Corinthians 6: 'in all things let us exhibit ourselves as the ministers of God,' and so on, 'in chastity, in sweetness, in the Holy Spirit. As chastised, and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.'

Jerome, to the virgin Demetrias: 'happy is that conscience of Christ, and blessed the virginity, in whose heart, besides the love of Christ, which is wisdom, chastity, patience, and justice, and the other virtues, no other love dwells, nor does it ever sigh at the remembrance of a man, nor desire to see one whom, once seen, it would be unwilling to let go.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, in the book On the Spirit and the Soul: 'nothing is more excellent, for a blessed life, than to turn within oneself, and be made a stranger to desires.'

Fourth, as the same Isidore says, it comes down to men's gardens, where it seeks food for itself; but once it has obtained food, it is accustomed to seek again the mountain ridges and the secret places of the woods.

It signifies contemplatives, given continually to heavenly things, apart from the moments needed for taking necessities. Luke 2: 'this widow lived to eighty-four years, who did not depart from the temple, serving God with fastings and prayers, night and day.'

An example is found in blessed Benedict, book 2 of Gregory's Dialogues, who remained three years in a cave, unknown except to a Roman monk, contemplating eternal things, and sighing for the heavenly, meditating on divine things, and spurning earthly ones.

Fifth, as the same Isidore says, it arrives in springtime, and, with a plaintive voice, announces and reveals the newness of the coming season. But in winter it loses its feathers, and then hides itself in the hollows of tree-trunks.

It signifies those who gladly and lovingly preach and announce to others, with sweet-flowing and most pure words, the pleasantness of the eternal, ever-green and ever-flowering paradise. But in this wretched present life they deprive themselves of every pleasure, and remove themselves from all the world's delights and vanities.

And this is what is said, Song of Songs 2: 'the flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning has come; the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land; the fig tree has put forth her green figs.'

It is sung of blessed Augustine, and is found in book 9 of the Confessions, that, having received the grace of baptism, he, together with his mother, at the mouth of the Tiber, spoke together, alone, most sweetly. And they reached out, with the mouth of the heart, together, toward the supernal streams of the fountain of life. And this world grew worthless amid their words and its delights. Then she said to her son: 'nothing now delights me in this life, since, having already scorned earthly happiness, I now see a servant of Christ.'

As Aristotle says, around springtime, its feathers regrown, coming out from the hidden places where it had lain, it builds fitting places for breeding, in which it broods over its eggs, breeds, and nourishes its chicks.

It signifies religious men who, at a fixed time, devote themselves mainly to solitude, and come forth at fixed times to give examples for the fruitfulness and salvation of souls, or for the conversion of sinners and the strengthening of the weak. 2 Corinthians 5: 'for whether we be transported in mind, it is to God; or whether we be sober, it is for you. For the charity of Christ presses us.'

Augustine, book 10 of the Confessions: 'terrified by my sins, and weighed down by the mass of my misery, I had turned this over in my heart, and had considered flight into solitude, but you forbade me, Lord, through your apostle, saying: therefore Christ died for all, that they who live may now not live to themselves, but to him who died for all.'
It is also sung of blessed Augustine: 'after his mother's death, Augustine returned to his own lands, where, devoting himself to holy readings and prayers, he wrote books and taught the unlearned.'
...blessed Ambrose, as is found in the Confessions of Augustine.
It lives and broods for fifteen years.

It signifies that contemplatives live and delight in mind according to the fifteen perfect and graduated ascents of the virtues, above the mind, which are mystically contained in the canticle of the fifteen degrees in the Psalter. Psalm 83: 'blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has disposed ascensions in his heart, in the vale of tears, in the place which he has set.'
'For the lawgiver will give a blessing, they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.'

Blessed Jerome relates an example, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, of twelve hermits dwelling near each other in the desert, who, once gathered together, said to one another what each meditated on chiefly, of whom the eighth said: 'I, turning over in my mind the empyrean heaven, contemplate the Lord of glory, shining, in the midst of the intellectual powers, above them all.' The others too, one by one, declared their own graces, in a similar but different way.

Eighth, as the same Aristotle says, it never descends upon a foul thing, nor upon a carcass; for it does not feed on carrion, but seeks, for its own food and that of its young, a few clean grains, and gathers them in clean places, where it lives.

It signifies holy men, leading their lives in poverty and cleanness, from their own just labor, never from another's, or from something base or basely acquired: 'and having food, and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content.'
Ephesians 4: 'he that stole, let him now steal no more; but rather let him labor, working with his hands, that he may have something to give to him that suffers need.'
Peter, to Clement, in the Itinerary: 'bread alone, with olives, and rarely also with vegetables, is my usual food. As for clothing, this that you see is a tunic with a cloak,' and so on.
Ninth, as the same Aristotle says, while other birds cry out, it groans.
It signifies the penitent man who, while worldly men exult, devotes himself to groaning. 'Like the young of the swallow, so will I cry, and I will meditate like a dove.'
'We groan, meditating like doves.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that 'he sought solitary places, friendly to sorrow, in which, with unspeakable groanings, he ceaselessly besought God, and, after a long persistence in prayer, deserved to be heard by the Lord.'
As the same Aristotle says, it builds its nest from small dry sticks, or twigs, low, poor, and stiff.

It signifies the evangelical man, content with a small and despised dwelling. Ecclesiasticus 29: 'better is the living of a poor man under a shelter of boards, than sumptuous fare,' and so on; there too: 'let a little be pleasing to you instead of much,' and so on.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis, Vita sancti Hilarionis abbatis in Palestina Hieronymi

cit.quote: An example is found in blessed Hilarion, of whom blessed Jerome writes, in his Life, that he lay on a bed of rushes until his death, and his dwelling was so small and narrow that it seemed more a tomb than a hut.
Once its mate has died, it never again settles on a green branch, nor drinks water unless it is troubled.

It signifies that a Christian, considering the death of Christ, who is joined and conformed to us in humanity, should never wish to rejoice in a worldly way, but always wish, in his inmost heart, to be transformed, in compassion, toward the crucified one. Philippians 3: 'for Christ's sake, I have counted all things as loss; and I esteem them as dung.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that he lamented Christ's passion as though it were always set before him, gazing at the crucified one with groaning mind and groaning eyes, and counted this whole universe as nothing.

As Constantine says, the chicks of the turtledove are hot and moist, which their heaviness in flying attests; but, once they begin to fly, they lose that heaviness, and their flesh becomes lighter and more agreeable to digest.

It signifies those who, although prone by nature to wrath and lust, procure for themselves gentleness and chastity through holy desires and diligent exercise of the virtues, and heavenly increase of lofty merits. Matthew: 'from the days of John the Baptist, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent bear it away.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, De officiis ministrorum Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose, On the Duties of Ministers, and elsewhere: 'everyone claims dignity for himself by grace, not by nature; by virtue, not by nobility of birth.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: Bernard, to Eugenius: 'the lineage of the apostles is proven noble by nothing else than the nobility of their character.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Chrysostomus, Homilie super Mattheum Iohannis Chrysostomi

cit.quote: Chrysostom, on Matthew, homily 44: 'there is one true nobility, namely, to do the will of God.'
Thirteenth, as the same Constantine puts it, the blood of its right wing is medicinal, just as the blood of the swallow and of the dove.
It signifies that the blood of Christ's passion is a medicine against all spiritual infirmities. Hebrews 9: 'the blood of Christ will cleanse our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God.'
Augustine, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'whomever the cunning of Satan has bitten, let him look upon Christ hanging on the wood; for there death was slain; the Lord lives forever.'
The vulture is found, according to the doctors, to have these properties, or conditions.
For first, as Isidore says, it is so named from its slow flight, as it were flying slowly. For, because of the great bulk of its flesh, it does not have swift flight.

It signifies those who become slow and lazy in rising toward God, or toward worthy works, on account of the abundance of carnality within them, which drives away from itself the spirit of grace. Wisdom 1: 'wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins. For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding.'
'For the corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presses down the mind that muses upon many things.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Augustine, On the Spirit and the Soul: 'bodily delight hinders the knowledge of spiritual good.'
Augustine, Against Julian: 'the movement of pleasure, being greatest, is likewise most hostile to lust; for bodily delight cannot agree with understanding.'

Second, as the same Isidore says, and blessed Ambrose in the Hexameron, vultures are said not to mate, but to conceive and be conceived, and to beget and be born, without coupling. For they do this by scent alone.

They signify virgins, begotten and begetting for God, without the foulness of carnal union, in fruits of the everlasting flowering and sweet-smelling delights of paradise. Ecclesiasticus 15: 'he that is a keeper of the law of justice shall get the mastery of her, and she will meet him as an honorable mother, and will receive him as a wife married of a virgin.'
'Come over to me,' says the Blessed Virgin Mary, 'all you that desire me, and be filled with my fruits. I am the mother of fair love.'

Fulgentius, in the sermon On All Saints, third lesson: 'the blessed mother of God, ever Virgin Mary, temple of the Lord, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, virgin before childbirth and virgin after childbirth; forming a godly people, she admonished them to spurn the perishing luxuries of the world, to turn away from the enticements of mortal nature, and to keep the purity of the flesh, together with the honor of virginity, within the lodgings of the heart, and affirmed that she was the queen of all virtues, the fruit of everlasting salvation, and a companion of the angels, by her own examples, so that a multitude of both sexes might imitate her.'
Third, as Isidore puts it, vultures live for a hundred years.
They signify perseverance in justice, even to the palm of martyrdom. Ecclesiasticus 4: 'strive for justice for your soul, and contend even unto death for justice.'

...martyrs, on account of the fullness of the life they have attained, or the perfect contempt of death, or the ready flight from the left hand of this life to the right hand of the homeland; virgins, on account of leisure and the perfection of integrity, by which they do not fight against the habit of the flesh; widows, in whom there is a great struggle, lest they be overcome by desire.

But Jerome, in the Apology to Pammachius, treating this same saying, speaks thus: 'thirty is referred to marriage, since the very joining of the fingers, as though embracing and binding itself in a soft kiss, marks the husband and the wife. But sixty is referred to widows, since they are placed in tribulation and distress; hence they are pressed down by the higher finger; and the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the enticements of a pleasure once known, the greater the reward. Further — I beg the diligent reader to attend — the number a hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right, and, with these same fingers, though not the same hand, by which married women and widows are signified on the left, it forms a circle, expressing the crown of virginity.' And below, in the same place: 'and certainly we have been much more indulgent toward marriage than almost all the Latin and Greek commentators, who refer the number a hundred to martyrs, sixty to virgins, but thirty to widows. And so it happens that husbands are excluded from the good earth and the seed of the father of the household.' Thus far Jerome. Whichever of these two ways, then, we wish to apply our moral reading of the hundred, we have, behold, a fitting path.

Fourth, as Pliny says, it is unkind toward its own young, like the kite too. For when it sees them growing fat, it strikes them with beak and feet, so that they become lean from the pain of the bites.

It signifies those who grow sad at the good fortune, or prosperous successes, of an Abel-like brother, as Cain did concerning Abel, Genesis 4, and the brothers of Joseph, Genesis 37; against which, 'charity is kind; it seeks not its own. It does not rejoice at iniquity, but rejoices with the truth.'
John the Evangelist, who rejoiced most of all when he felt his children growing in Christ, as is found near the beginning of 2 John and in the accounts of his deeds.

Fifth, as the same Pliny says, vultures are especially strong in their sense of smell; hence they perceive the smell of carcasses from far off. For those existing beyond the sea perceive them on this side, and conversely; hence an army is followed by vulture upon vulture, as it were, to be sated on the corpses of men as well as horses. According to the augurs, too, when many vultures gather and fly about, it is an omen of a coming battle, which they foresee, by some hidden natural sense, is going to happen.

It signifies certain gluttons, or even entertainers, who, wherever weddings, or courts, or carnal feasts take place, or wherever they know there is an opportunity to fill their belly, or gain some temporal profit, run there anxiously and gorge themselves; and when they multiply, it is a sign of the multiplication of crimes, and, consequently, of infernal punishments. The letter of Jude: 'these are spots in their banquets, feasting together without fear, feeding themselves, clouds without water, which are carried about by the winds; to whom the storm of darkness is reserved forever.'
Bernard, in his sermons: 'the pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Likewise, Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'the life of men is midway between the life of angels and of cattle, so that those who savor according to the spirit are made like the angels, but those who feel according to the flesh are joined with the beasts.'
'Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless cattle, and made like to them.'
As Aristotle says, the vulture fights with the heron, and flies over it, and, when it defeats it, it dies.

It signifies attackers of good men, deserving, by this very act, eternal death, and sometimes temporal death too, as is clear in the two companies of fifty men, sent to seize Elijah, who was troubling them, devoured by fire from heaven, 2 Kings 1.
An example is found in the tyrant Aegeas, adversary of blessed Andrew, and the tyrant Paschasius, adversary of blessed Lucy, and many others, as is found in the Ecclesiastical Acts.
...a bird of raw flesh, and so it fights against other birds for food.

It signifies detractors, attacking holy men out of envy, or to fulfill their own evil will. Micah 3: 'they bite with their teeth, and preach peace; and if any man gives not something for their mouths, they prepare war against him.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'A cursed tongue strikes charity in all who hear it, and, as far as lies in it, thoroughly kills and extinguishes it.'

Eighth, as Aristotle says, it hunts from noon until night, and rests from sunrise until that hour; and when it grows old, its beak lengthens above, and curves at the tip, and finally it dies of hunger.

It signifies the greedy, who press after temporal gains from youth even to death, and, never satisfied, in the end come to eternal damnation. Ecclesiastes 4: 'considering, I found also another vanity under the sun: there is but one, and he has not a second, no child, nor brother, and yet he ceases not to labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with riches; neither does he reflect, saying: for whom do I labor, and defraud my soul of good things?'
Psalm 75: 'they have slept their sleep; and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands.'
Luke 16, of him who, as the Church sings, asked for a drop of water, since he had denied crumbs of bread to Lazarus the beggar.

As the same Aristotle says, when it has some food left over, it does not leave anything for other birds, as the eagle does, but stores it in the nest, to feed its chicks, since it does not easily obtain food.

It signifies the rich, and men of this kind, who leave nothing for the poor, and are unwilling even to give their leftovers to needy neighbors, but turn everything to their own private benefit and carnal love, saying that temporal goods of this kind are not easily gotten. Job 15: 'there was nothing left of his food. Therefore nothing of his goods shall remain.'

...the emperor Decius, and Julian the Apostate, who, as history relates, held the poor in hatred, and had compassion on no one afflicted — indeed, they added to their affliction, whereas to persecute the poor is the height of savagery, as the Gloss says on Psalm 69: 'O God, come to my assistance.'
As the same Aristotle says, it nests on high mountains and in dense groves.

It signifies the proud and the ambitious, walking in things great and marvelous, above themselves. Isaiah 14: 'I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, and in his sermons and letters: 'every proud man is utterly unbearable; his manner of dress is excessive, his gait pompous, his neck stiff, he strives from a loftier place, and desires to be preferred to his betters; he boasts of his own opinions and his own deeds, and keeps no reverence in his service.'
Eleventh, as the same Aristotle says, if it sees anything flying around its young, it strikes it with its beak, and drives it off.

It signifies those who claim their goods as their own private possession, denying them to the common charity of their neighbors. Philippians 2: 'for all seek the things that are their own, not the things that are Jesus Christ's.'
Nabal of Carmel, 1 Kings 25, who, for this reason, died an evil death.
Such were Antiochus, 2 Maccabees 7, and Ahab, 1 Kings 17, and many others.

As the same Aristotle says, it feeds its chicks until they can fly, and then casts them from the nest, and forbids them to approach that place, nor does it allow one pair of vultures to enter the place of another.

It signifies those who, though they could be hospitable, refuse to be, and, once they have fed the poor man even once, no longer wish to see him again; against which: 'let brotherly charity remain among you, and forget not hospitality, for by this some, unknowingly, have received angels as guests.'

Against those unwilling to help travelers, blessed Jerome relates, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, that there was a man and his wife who divided all their substance and gain among the poor: first, among travelers; second, for their own use; third, among those living in virginity. They lay clothed in sackcloth at night, and it was revealed to two holy fathers, who wished to know their own merits, that they had not attained their measure.

There is a certain species of river-bird called the almachar, which fears the vulture, and so flees to the water, while the vulture flies around at a distance; and, since it has keen eyes, it watches for when that bird leaves the water, and then, if it can, seizes it.

It signifies the cunning of the devil, by which he strives to overcome the men of God, according to that saying, 1 Peter 5: 'be sober, and watch, because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about, seeking whom he may devour.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus, Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in the sermon On the Circumcision: 'the ancient enemy does not cease to press on, so as to corrupt, by whatever means, the faith of Christians, or the faithful. He knows to whom he should offer the incitements of lust, the heat of desire; to whom he should pour in the poison of envy; to whom he should show the poisons of deceit. He knows whom to deceive with joy, whom to trouble with sorrow. He has certain ones among them whom he has bound to himself so tightly that he makes use of their wits and their tongues for the deception of others.'
As the same author says, it is a very foul-smelling and unclean bird.

It signifies the unclean life of the lustful and the wanton. Philippians 3: 'for many walk, of whom I have told you often (and now tell you weeping), that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.' Such men cannot grasp or savor divine or heavenly and intellectual things.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis, Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs, and elsewhere: 'divine consolation is a delicate thing, which is not given to those who possess what belongs to another.'
As the same author says, its flesh is very hard, of bad flavor and heavy odor, and so is useless for food.

It signifies the life of certain evil, or depraved and perverse men, whose life is of bad composition in conscience, of bad edification in life, and of bad reputation in fame, and so fruitless in every way for the Church. 2 Timothy 2: 'of whom is Philetus and Hymenaeus, who have fallen from the truth, saying that the resurrection is past already, and have subverted the faith of some. But the sure foundation of God stands firm, having this seal: the Lord knows who are his.'

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: Nicholas, the newcomer from Antioch, and Torquatus, the betrayer of Tiburtius, Julian the Apostate, and Muhammad, and similar members of the devil, of whom their own accounts speak.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: As Gregory says, on Job, it easily comes down to earth for a carcass, but, once it has come down from the earth, it scarcely rises again.

It signifies money to hypocrites, or the greedy, who, for a small thing, seek earthly gain, and, once the desire or pursuit of earthly things has taken root in their affections, scarcely return to salutary things. Ecclesiasticus 10: 'there is not a more wicked thing than to love money; for such a one sets even his own soul to sale, since, while he lives, he has cast away his innermost parts.'

Concerning this, blessed Jerome relates, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, that there was a certain holy gardener who, apart from what he needed for his own use, spent all his gains on the poor, and was healthy. And the devil put into his heart the desire to gather money, lest he perhaps fall ill and be in want; and afterward he did fall ill, and his foot was to be cut off, unless, led by penitence, he was healed by God before the physician arrived.
As the same author says, flying high, it spies a carcass far below, and, for love of the carcass, lowers itself from the height of the air.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: It signifies the Son of God Most High, according to blessed Gregory in the Moralia, who, existing in the bosom of the Father, and, seeing the human race made, as it were, a corpse because of Adam's sin, though he was in the form of God, out of pity took flesh from the Virgin, and came down to it, to incorporate it into himself. But while he was drawing it to himself, the adversaries of the people who came upon him, namely the Jews, seized him like a vulture, and killed him, as though blind, not turning aside, nor caring to know, the savior who was working salvation in the midst of their land.

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis, Enarrationes in Psalmos Augustini

cit.quote: Indeed, according to Augustine, on the Psalms, they, as though feverish with a great madness, raged against the physician who had come to heal them.

Job 28 says, of the Jewish people: 'the bird has not known the path, neither has the eye of the vulture beheld it,' since that blinded people scorned to turn aside to the ways of Christ, walking on earth in the manner of an angel, always lifted toward heavenly things, and did not care to consider his intention and his affection, in the manner of a vulture striving to incorporate the human race into himself and draw it to himself.
But whence they thought to cast him down, from there they exalted him, since, Proverbs 21: 'there is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.'
'Jesus, crowned with glory and honor, because of the suffering of death.'

Eighteenth, as the same author says, when it is hindered by something, it beats its wings against the wind, and so, by the wind's help rather than its own labor, lifts itself from the depths into the air.

It signifies contemplative and holy men who, enduring at times the troubles of temptations, and recognizing their own frailty, commit themselves entirely to the grace of the Holy Spirit, by whose worthy inspiration, lifted above the level of the mind toward heavenly things with all their desires, they overcome the depths of those very temptations, and triumph over all their trials. 2 Corinthians 2: 'let us not be deceived by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his devices. Now thanks be to God, who always makes us triumph in Christ Jesus.'
2 Corinthians 1: 'in all things we overcome, because of him that has loved us.'

The Master relates, in the Summa of Vices, that when a certain holy man was tempted with the sin of fornication, and could resist no longer, he prostrated himself before the crucifix, and said: 'the earth, or fortress, of my body, which I hold from you, I can no longer defend. I return it to you. You defend it.' And at once the temptation was overcome, and so the tempter withdrew, confounded.

bibl.author: Plinius maior, Historia naturalis Plinii Maioris

cit.quote: Among birds, the vulture is opposed to serpents. For if its feathers are burned, they drive off serpents with their smell. Its heart, too, keeps those who carry it safe from serpents and wild beasts. Its heart, likewise, bound in the skin of a lion or a wolf, drives off demons. Its feather, bound to the left foot of a woman in labor, quickly delivers her; but it ought to be loosened more quickly once the child begins to come forth, lest the afterbirth follow with it. An ointment made from the vulture's fat and oil of iris heals the sinews, and cures beasts of burden. Its right foot, bound to a painful left foot, heals it; likewise, the left heals the right. Its tongue, drawn out without iron and hung on the neck in a new cloth, is said to make a man pleasing, so as to obtain from another whatever he asks. The ash of its burned bones, mixed with celandine, heals the diseases of animals. Its blood, with the herb 'carabeote' and celandine, heals leprosy. Thus far Pliny, in the said book.

It signifies that holy men, and whatever is in their souls and bodies, and even in their garments and relics, fight for God and for truth, and are opposed to the devil and to all malice, or iniquity, and to every spiritual infirmity. Acts 5: 'and the multitude of men and women who believed in the Lord was more increased, so that they brought forth the sick into the streets, and laid them on beds and couches, that when Peter came, his shadow at the least might overshadow any of them, and they might be delivered from their infirmities. And there came also together a multitude out of the neighboring cities to Jerusalem, bringing sick persons, and such as were troubled with unclean spirits, who were all healed.'

'God worked no small miracles by the hand of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons were brought from his body to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the wicked spirits went out of them.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'do you wish to know the gifts of God? The garments of Paul were a terror to demons.'
Augustine, in the Confessions: 'let my tongue, Lord, and whatever I think, know, savor, and write, serve you.'
The screech-owl is found, according to the authorities, to have these conditions, or properties.
For first, as Isidore says, it is named from its wailing, or rather its screeching. For it screeches a great deal, especially by night, over buildings.

It signifies those who always lament and complain of poverty, or some other adversity, always laboring for their own relief, whom, on account of their persistence, one must sometimes satisfy. Luke 18: 'there was a judge in a certain city, who feared not God, nor regarded man. And there was a certain widow in that city, and she came to him, saying: avenge me of my adversary. And he would not for a long time. But afterward he said within himself: although I fear not God, nor regard man, yet because this widow is troublesome to me, I will avenge her, lest continually coming, she weary me.'

bibl.author: Vita sancti Iohannis Eleemosynarii episcopi Alexandrie

cit.quote: An example is found in those who, feigning themselves poor, deceived John the Almsgiver, the patriarch, as is related in his Life, and, because of their persistence, received something from him, but were nonetheless justly judged by divine judgment, as is found in the accounts of his deeds.
Second, as the same Isidore says, this bird, among the augurs, when it screeches a great deal, portends adversity; but, when silent, portends prosperity.

It signifies detractors who, when they detract greatly, bring, or foreshadow, their own damnation; but when they hold back, or restrain themselves, they do themselves good, and deserve to have God propitious to them.
For this reason the wise man says, Proverbs 24: 'my son, fear God, and the king, and have no fellowship with detractors, for their destruction shall rise suddenly, and who knows the ruin of both?'
'The north wind drives away rain, as does a sad countenance a backbiting tongue.'
'He that detracts from anything binds himself for the future, but he that fears the commandment shall dwell in peace.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'A heart bitter with the gall of envy cannot scatter, through the instrument of the tongue, anything but bitter things. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; and there are two kinds of this plague,' and so on. Thus far Bernard, in the same place.
As the same Isidore says, its voice is generally, according to the augurs, unlucky and hostile.

It signifies certain talkative men, multiplying words without reason, and bringing on others a certain misfortune, or a heavy tedium. Ecclesiasticus 27: 'much swearing shall fill the head with hair standing on end, and its irreverence will make one stop the ears. The talk of sinners is hateful, and their laughter is in the delights of sin.'
An example is found in Simon Magus, of whom the Itinerary speaks, and in many other similar men, in the Old Testament and in the New.
The hoopoe is found to have these conditions, or properties.
As Isidore says, it is a bird helmeted with crests rising from its head.
It signifies the proud, and those who make a show of themselves.

An example is found in the illustrious Antiochus, 1 Maccabees 1; against which, Esther 14: 'you know, Lord, that I abhor the sign of my pride, which is upon my head in the days of my public appearance, and detest it like a cloth stained with menstrual blood.'
It is written of blessed Bernard that he considered every honor shown to him as belonging equally to another.

Second, as the same Isidore says, it is a bird beautiful in its feathers and varied in color, but most filthy in its deeds. For it eats human dung, and dwells among dung-heaps or tombs, and therefore always stinks.
It signifies beasts of burden, that is, luxurious men appearing beautiful in their garments, but foul and stinking in soul and body, Joel 1: 'the beasts have rotted in their own dung.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus, Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'for beasts to rot in their own dung is for carnal men to end their life in the stench of luxury.'

Third, as the philosophers say, and as Isidore states, when it grows old, so that it can neither see nor fly, its chicks pluck out its weakened feathers, and anoint its eyes with the juices of herbs, and warm it beneath their wings until its feathers grow back. And so, fully renewed, it flies and sees clearly, just as they themselves do.

It signifies that works of piety are to be devoted, with great zeal, to one's parents. Ecclesiasticus 3: 'he that fears the Lord honors his parents, and will serve them as his masters that brought him into the world,' and so on.
Jerome, in a certain letter: 'love the superior of the monastery as a father, esteem him as a teacher, believe whatever he shall tell you.'
The bat is found to have these properties, or conditions, according to the authorities.
For first, as Isidore says, and as Ambrose touches on in the Hexameron, it took its name from the time of day, since, being blind, it flies about in the twilight of evening.

It signifies wandering, or wicked and overly curious men, who, deprived of the light of grace, always wish to learn, and never deserve to arrive at the knowledge of the truth, according to 2 Timothy 3: 'always learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of the truth.'

For this reason such men are called peripatetics, that is, followers of Aristotle, as it were always wandering about among the different schools and masters, but never finding themselves in the discovery of the truth, as a certain Gloss says, in the science below.
Second, as Constantine says, its blood, smeared on the eyelids, does not let hair grow back. For it clogs the pores, and, once they are clogged, hairs do not regrow.
It signifies that the blood of Christ represses the thoughts of the old life from man's understanding, Hebrews 9: 'the blood of Christ will cleanse our conscience from dead works.'
Whoever — Augustine, in the sermon On a Single Martyr: 'whomever the cunning of Satan has bitten, let him look upon Christ hanging on the wood,' and so on.
Third, as the Gloss on Isaiah 2 says, it sucks the oil from lamps, and hides itself in the crevices of walls.

It signifies mercenary clerics and religious who, once they have received their ecclesiastical portion, withdraw themselves from usefulness and common service, and secretly devote themselves to unspeakable deeds.
Of the priest Eli, 1 Kings 2; Ephesians 5: 'the things that are done by them in secret, it is a shame even to speak of.'
Of clerics and monks common in our own time, and especially in the priest who opposed blessed Benedict, of whom blessed Gregory tells in the second book of the Dialogues.
Fish, both in general and in particular, are found to have these conditions, or properties; for they are first considered in general.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: For first, as Isidore says, in book 12, chapter 6, they are called 'pisces,' whence also 'pecus' (cattle), from feeding; for they lick the earth and the water-plants. They are also called 'reptiles,' since in swimming they have a kind of creeping, or crawling, appearance. For in swimming they crawl, although they plunge into the depths.

They signify students feeding and refreshing themselves, humbly, in the deep and varied waters of the sacred Scriptures, knowing what is written, Proverbs 11: 'where there is humility, there also is wisdom.'
'The sea' — supply, of sacred Scripture — 'is great and wide; there the creeping things, that is, the students, of which there is no number.'
Likewise Psalm 106: 'they that go down to the sea in ships, doing business in many waters; these have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep.'

'I exhort you not to be slow in devoting care to the true and holy Scriptures. For it is a sincere and solid thing, and nothing empty or wavering rings from it. I especially urge you to read the tongues of the apostles; for from these you will be roused to know the prophets, whose testimonies the apostles use.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Paulinum presbyterum

cit.quote: 'I beg you, dearest brother, to live among the divine words, to meditate upon them; to know nothing else, to seek nothing else. Does it not seem to you already, here on earth, a dwelling-place of the heavenly kingdom? Let us learn on earth those things whose knowledge will endure for us in heaven.'

Second, as blessed Ambrose says in the Hexameron, they have a great neighborliness and kinship with the waters. For outside the waters they cannot live long, nor do they live long by the mere breathing of air, without the drawing-in of water. For they have a certain crawling appearance and nature.

They signify that students in various sciences ought to be familiar with, and joined in devotion to, religious and other holy and learned men, abounding in heavenly grace and overflowing with the teaching of the Gospel, if they wish to attain to the grace of God and their own final salvation, and to be useful to the Church, Ecclesiasticus 4: 'make yourself affable to the congregation of the poor.' And again, in the seventh chapter of the same: 'stand in the multitude of wise elders, and join yourself from your heart to their wisdom, that you may hear every discourse of God, and the proverbs of praise may not escape you. If you see a man of understanding, watch for him, and let your foot wear the steps of his doors.'

An example is found in blessed Augustine, who, by the familiarity of blessed Ambrose, deserved to be converted and enlightened by the prerogative of heavenly grace and wisdom, as is found in Augustine's book of the Confessions.

Augustine, On Christian Doctrine: 'it seems to me that studious and freeborn young men ought to be advised not to dare to follow any teachings practiced outside the Church of Christ, as if they might attain to the blessed life by them.'

bibl.author: Aulus Gellius Noctes Attice Auli Gellii

cit.quote: Aulus Gellius, book 7, chapter 10: 'Euclid the philosopher, having changed his dress, used to go a thousand paces by night to hear Socrates.'

Third, as Avicenna says, in book 2, chapter 7, fish that dwell in rocky places are better and more flavorful. Likewise, and in the same way, those that dwell in running waters, in which there is no filth or mud, are better than those of open plains or of lakes.

It signifies that religious, or apostles, living as citizens in poverty and austerity, and ever conversing in the venerable Scriptures that make one hasten toward and unto God, are more useful to the Church and more virtuous than every other soul. An example is found in Paul and Augustine, Ambrose and Jerome and Gregory, and other lovers of poverty and austerity and dwellers in the holy Scriptures, and how many peoples they converted, and how many souls they made hasten toward God by example and by word.
As the same Avicenna says, in the same place, fish nourished in the deep sea are more praiseworthy than others, not elsewhere.

It signifies that those who have given themselves and their affection wholly to the profundity of sacred theology alone, and have from childhood conversed in it out of love, are worthy of greater praise, Wisdom 8: 'I have loved wisdom, and have sought her out from my youth, and have desired to take her for my spouse, and I became a lover of her beauty. On account of her I shall have glory among the multitudes, and honor with the elders, though I be young, and I shall be found of a quick understanding in judgment, and shall be admired in the sight of the mighty, and the faces of princes shall wonder at me.'
An example is found in Timothy, who, as is found in 2 Timothy 3, 'knew the holy Scriptures from his infancy,' and so was instructed, perfected, and prepared for every good work and teaching.
Fifth, as the same Avicenna says, fish that dwell in open waters, exposed above to the blowing of the winds, are better than those which are the opposite.

They signify those who walk in the light and are exercised by adversities, and are proven to be worthy of more abundant praise and blessedness, James 1: 'blessed is the man that endures temptation; for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life,' and so on.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: 'Good is the tribulation that makes us worthy to be heard by the Lord in a large place. For as spices give forth their fragrance only when set on fire, so holy men make known, in tribulations, all the sweetness of the virtues that is in them. For the Lord's mercy is commanded by day, since it is bidden to be known in a time of tranquility; but by night it is declared, since the gift that is received in tranquility is manifested in tribulations.'
An example is found in the paralyzed servant of whom blessed Gregory writes, in the Dialogues, that he was of wondrous patience in his continual pains, even unto death.

Likewise of that holy old man of whom blessed Jerome tells, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, that he thought himself abandoned by God in that year in which he was not gravely afflicted with illness; and of many others, such as Job and Tobit, who were each of wondrous patience in their temptations and adversities.

Sixth, as the same Avicenna says, in the same place, fish, whether of the sea or elsewhere, are better in the northern and eastern sea than in the southern, because, by the impetuous blowing of the winds, the waters are more moved and more purified and refined, and so the fish of those waters are more moved and exercised, and cleansed of their own superfluities.

They signify that martyrs and other servants of God, afflicted for Christ and exposed and exercised by the deep persecutions of tyrants, were purged, above all, of every impurity and defect, and so, proved and examined like gold, entered into eternal glory. 'The furnace tries the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation just men,' Ecclesiasticus 27.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie XL in Evangelia Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the homily on the Gospel 'This is my commandment': 'behold, the chosen of God tame the flesh, strengthen the spirit, gleam with virtues, command demons, preach their eternal homeland with voice and character. They love that homeland even by dying, and reach it through torments.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio psalmi CXVIII Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on 'Blessed are the undefiled': 'the greater the tribulations have been, the more abundant a consolation is reserved.'
An example is found in blessed Lawrence and Vincent, who obtained special crowns of glory for this.

As the same Avicenna says, fish of lakes, and especially those far removed from a river or the sea, are bad and weak and of bad flavor, and quickly rot. For they have stillness, and their corruption is not washed away by an inflowing river or the sea.
It signifies that those who are not exercised in good works quickly perish, and are exposed to every spiritual infirmity, who withdraw themselves from the Gospel and from the bitterness of penance.
'For idleness is the teacher of all evils,' Ecclesiasticus 33: 'for idleness has taught much evil.'
The poet: 'it is asked: why did Aegisthus become an adulterer? The cause is plain: he was idle.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis Epistola Hieronymi ad Nepotianum presbyterum

cit.quote: There was a Greek youth in a monastery who, by no abstinence, by no greatness of labor, could extinguish the flame of the flesh. The father of the monastery preserved this endangered youth by this device. He commands a certain very grave man to assail the youth with quarrels and reproaches, and, after inflicting these injuries, to come first to make complaints against him. Witnesses, called, spoke against him in favor of the one who had done the wrong. The youth began to weep against the lie; no one else would believe the truth; the father alone cleverly labored to plead his defense, lest the brother be overwhelmed by too great a sadness. To be brief: a year was spent thus, at the end of which the youth, questioned about his former thoughts, replied: 'ah, it is not permitted me to live, yet I long to fornicate.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Eighth, as Isidore says, in book 12, it is, for all fish generally, a sign of death when they turn their belly upward, and it is an infallible sign of death when they float on the surface of the water.

It signifies that when cloistered men delight in the things of the belly, and especially outside the cloister, it is a sign and proof of their spiritual death; against which, Ecclesiasticus 29: 'better is the fare of the poor man under a covering of boards, than sumptuous banquets in another's house, without a home.'

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: 'I judge it the first proof of a well-composed mind to be able to remain with itself, and to dwell with itself.' An example is found in two monks of Saint Benedict who, against the institutes of the rule, ate outside the monastery.

Ninth, as the same says, many fish, going out from the sea into fresh waters, delight and grow fat in fresh water; and conversely there are some that dwell now in the sea, now in fresh water. But there are many river-fish which, not enduring the saltness of the sea, die suddenly upon tasting salt water.

They signify good men of the world who, out of affection, run to the familiarity and teaching of religious, and delight spiritually in their word and example, and grow fat with the grace of God, so that, detesting the sea of this world after their experience of it and of its vices and dangers, they at last die to the world in Christ, Ecclesiasticus 9: 'let just men be your guests, and let your glory be in the fear of God; and let all your discourse be on the commandments of the Most High.'
'For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.'
An example is found in the emperor Theodoret, who greatly profited by the familiarity of blessed Ambrose, as is found in the Tripartite History.

Likewise an example is found in the emperor Constantine who, as is found in the deeds of Saint Sylvester and in the Tripartite History, greatly profited by his intercourse with him, so that both died to the world, and yet died in Christ.

Tenth, as the same Isidore says, there are certain fish, and many of them, that live partly in the waters, partly on land, and retain by nature the office both of swimming in the waters and of walking on land; for by night they go out to grassy pastures, but by day they remain in the waters.

They signify evangelical religious, who now ascend, in mind above the mind, to the pastures of eternal greenness, now condescend piously to build up and instruct the peoples; for 'many waters' are 'many peoples,' Revelation 17.
This same thing is signified wholly by Jacob's ladder, Genesis 28, on which angels were seen ascending and descending.

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum

cit.quote: It is written of blessed Francis, in his Life, that on Jacob's ladder he was accustomed to climb by night to God of heaven, presenting himself to him in mind, but by day to descend, building up his brothers.
We also have an example, much greater, in Christ, who, as is found, Luke 21, was by day teaching in the temple, but by night lodged on the Mount of Olives, and so on.

bibl.author: Basilius Cesariensis Homilie in Hexameron Basilii Cesariensis

cit.quote: Eleventh, as Basil says in the Hexameron, book 8, chapter 3, the kinds of fish are distinguished. For some are of the open sea, some of the shore, some wide-ranging, some of the rocks, some gregarious, some monstrous, some huge, some tiny.

They signify the various ranks of men in the ecclesiastical hierarchy, or the varieties of religious orders, 1 Corinthians 12: 'God has placed some in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, third powers, then the graces of healing, helps, governments, kinds of tongues, interpretations of speeches.'

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De celesti hierarchia

cit.quote: Whence Dionysius says, in the Angelic Hierarchy, that the distribution of gifts is according to the fittingness of degrees and orders, and not only in the hierarchy but also within an order, some exceed and excel others, and the angels refer their operations not only to God but also to the higher orders.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: As the same Isidore says, in the same place, fish also have their own proper lot and their own proper nature, and a differing food, and a fixed condition of living, so that on this account no water-creature ever becomes tame, nor suffers itself to be handled by the hands of men.

It signifies the state and condition of anchorites who, fleeing the sight of men, lie open and free for the monastic contemplation of heavenly things, and enjoy the singular sweetnesses of the Holy Spirit's refreshments and anointings, according to that saying: 'for what have I in heaven, and besides you what do I desire upon earth? My flesh and my heart have fainted away; you are the God of my heart, and my portion, God, forever.'
'It is good for a man, when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit solitary, and hold his peace, because he has taken it up upon himself.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: ...of the fathers in the wilderness of Egypt, as blessed Jerome relates in the Lives of the Fathers, and blessed Ambrose On Paradise.

As Aristotle says, book 7, fish in winter flee from the depths of the sea toward the shore, seeking warmth, and there they seek their food. But in summer, on the contrary, they flee from the shores into the depths, which have less heat; for excessive heat harms them.

They signify religious who despise worldly things and desire eternal ones, knowing and understanding that the love of the world, wickedly inflaming, harms salvation, and so is to be fled above all, and one must cling to divine love, Philippians 3: 'I count all things to be but loss, for the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord; for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them as dung, that I may gain Christ.'

bibl.author: Hugo de Sancto Victore De laude caritatis Hugonis de Sancto Victore

cit.quote: Hugh of Saint Victor, On the Praise of Charity: 'the signs of those who have charity are these: to forsake the world, to escape scandals, to scorn the glory of this world, to lift up one's desires toward heavenly things.'

As the same Aristotle says, in the same place, chapter 5, there is great diversity in the manner of living of fish, and even an exceeding variety in the succession of each kind. For, in general, they do not brood over their eggs as birds do, nor build nests, nor with labor nourish their own young, but the water, receiving the egg, makes it a living creature, and the offspring, once infused, remains unchanging within each kind toward another nature, and is not, as with many land animals, corrupted in its likeness and appearance by adulterous mingling.

They signify that among religious, in comparison with those of the world, there is a great difference of character and of deeds, and the old are succeeded by the new, and religion itself, without much human industry, makes those who are converted and sent by God, by divine grace, into perfect men, unchangeable from their profession once assumed, and having received heavenly grace, and never deceivable by the world or the devil, or by the corrupting temptation of the flesh, Romans 8: 'the Spirit himself gives testimony to our spirit that we are the sons of God. Who then shall separate us from the charity of Christ?'
Jerome, in a letter — Jerome, letter 64 — tells of five thousand monks dwelling in various cells under heavenly discipline.
Augustine, in the book of the Confessions, tells that at Milan there was a monastery full of such brothers under Ambrose, its nourisher.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Ambrose also says, in the book On Paradise, that under father Pachomius there were fifteen hundred such servants of God under the discipline of the anointing.

bibl.author: Basilius Cesariensis Homilie in Hexameron Basilii Cesariensis

cit.quote: Fifteenth, as the same Basil says, in the same place, chapter 5, there are certain innumerable fish which, as though by some common decree, set out on the labor of a journey for the sake of food beyond their own waters, and all together, as though at a given signal, depart for distant places. For when the time of spawning begins to press, some, roused by others through the laws of nature, at once make for the regions of the northern sea. And when you see them returning, gathered in a very dense mass, you would think a most violent torrent was flowing along the shore of the Propontis, streaming out toward the sea.

They signify religious holding property in common, who, dwelling under abbots and priors, going out to their tasks on fixed days and hours at a given signal, and returning, are found, on account of the good of obedience, to be rewarded both in spiritual merits and in temporal goods, with divine approval, Psalm 103: 'the sun arose, and they were gathered together, and they shall lie down in their dens. Man shall go forth to his work, and to his labor, until the evening,' and so on; 'how great are your works, Lord! You have made all things in wisdom; the earth is full of your possessions.' It is told, by men worthy of trust, that in the time of blessed Bernard, in the monastery, all the monks commonly and gladly went out to their labors except one or two lazy and unruly ones. Some, however, returning late, found before the monastery the Blessed Virgin, holding in her hand a box with an excellent electuary, and gave a spoonful to each. But when the unruly one, or ones, came to receive their portion, they heard from her, with shame, this sentence: 'he who does not work, let him not eat.'

bibl.author: Basilius Cesariensis Homilie in Hexameron Basilii Cesariensis

cit.quote: As the same Basil says, in the same book and chapter, one kind of food is fitted to one kind of fish, and another to another. For some are nourished by mud, some are content with the worms born in the water, but most are satisfied by devouring one another in turn, and among them the smaller is always food for the other, that is, for the larger. And if it should happen that the one who had caught the smaller is himself seized in the bite of a stronger one, each then supports the other that comes after.

It signifies those who oppress their inferiors by their power, against which the apostle speaks, 1 Thessalonians 4: 'let no man overreach, nor circumvent his brother in business, because the Lord is the avenger of all these things, as we have told you before, and have testified.'

bibl.author: Basilius Cesariensis Homilie in Hexameron Basilii Cesariensis

cit.quote: How does that man differ from that basest of fish, who, inflamed by the love of riches, has swallowed up the poor he has caught in the insatiable jaws of his own rapacity? Another kept back, by force, the substance he had taken from a poor man. A certain man made him, by threats and terrors, give back his own inheritance, and so he was convicted of being more unjust than the just man he had wronged, and more rapacious than the robber. Beware, then, lest the same fate that befalls fish should overtake you, that is, the hook, or the net, or the basket.
Seventeenth, as Avicenna says, book 2, fish that feed on good herbs and the roots of plants are better for use than those that feed on flowing filth.

It signifies that theologians, who feed on the divine books and the original writings of the saints, are better than lawyers or artists who feed on the writings of worldly authors and worldly deeds, Philippians 3: 'I count all things to be but loss, for the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord,' and so on.

Whence blessed Augustine says, in book 4 of the Confessions, that a soul, wearied at last by deceptions, ought to commit to the truth whatever it has from the truth, and it will lose nothing. For a good thing profits nothing to one who does not use it well.

Eighteenth, as Aristotle says, book 2, fish that are not very large, and do not have flesh too hard and dry, and in which there is not excessive fat or sliminess, and in which there is no bad flavor or smell.
It signifies the humble and the abstinent, more fitted for grace and good repute, James 4: 'God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.'
...bearing about in our body, that the life of Jesus also may be made manifest in our mortal flesh. An example is found in blessed Francis, who was most eager for these two virtues.
Fish that have hard flesh become better when salted.
