It signifies that those who are too hard are of no use unless they are seasoned with the salt of discretion, Colossians 4: 'walk in wisdom. Let your speech be always seasoned with the salt of grace, that it may give grace to those who hear it.'
The Canon says: 'that man will do all manner of evil to another who is harsh and cruel to himself.'
Twentieth, as the same Avicenna says, every fish in general is cold and moist.

It signifies that all religious ought to be cold in chastity and moist in piety and devotion, 2 Corinthians 6: 'in all things let us exhibit ourselves as the ministers of God, in chastity, in charity, in sweetness, in the Holy Spirit.'
Gregory, in the second book of the Dialogues.

Twenty-first, as the same Avicenna says, salted fish are more fitting for medicine; for the heads of salted fish heal the bites of a rabid dog and the stings of scorpions; they root out proud flesh in ulcers, and are of benefit to putrid and running sores.

They signify that the discreet, and those mortified in the flesh, are especially fitting, indeed chiefly profitable, for the instruction and edification of sinners and of those weak in spirit, 2 Corinthians 4: 'we who live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake,' and so on; and below, chapter 5: 'whether we be transported in mind, it is to God; or whether we be sober, it is for you; for the charity of Christ presses us.'
'I am made all things to all men, that I might save all.'

It is written of blessed Ambrose, a most discreet man, in his Life, that he was of such piety that if anyone confessed his sins to him, he wept, so strongly compassionating, that he truly compelled the very sinner who was confessing to tears of contrition, and thus he healed them all.
Twenty-second, as the same author states, the broth of every fish is of benefit against poisons drunk and against stings.
It signifies the life and memory of perfect and holy religious men, and their virtues and relics, useful and virtuous to others.
Of Peter, whose shadow healed all infirmities, as is found in Acts 5.
...demons.
Do you wish to know the gifts of God? Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'the garments of Paul were a terror to demons.'
Twenty-third, as Aristotle states, book 7, fish generally labor more by day than by night, and more before midnight than after.
And therefore, as the same author says, they hunt before sunrise, for which reason hunters then set their nets, since fish do not see well at that hour.

bibl.author: Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Thessalonicenses prima

cit.quote: They signify that religious and holy men walk in truth and light more than hypocrites and the false, and are for that reason assailed and tried by demons, especially when they find some occasion; wherefore the apostle says, 1 Thessalonians 5: 'we are not children of the night, nor of darkness, but of the day.'

bibl.author: Leo Magnus Tractatus septem et nonaginta Leonis Magni

cit.quote: Pope Leo, in the sermon On the Circumcision: 'for the ancient enemy does not cease to spread everywhere the snares of deception, and to press on, so that by whatever means he may corrupt the faith of believers.'
Twenty-fourth, as the same Aristotle says, book 4, at night fish seek their food and delight in fragrant things, for they smell and hear.

They signify contemplatives, and men of prayer and devotion, that especially by night they devote themselves to the refreshment of the spirit, and suspend their inner sense of smell toward heavenly fragrances, and their hearing toward heavenly harmonies, and delight in inward consolations, Psalm 91: 'it is good to give praise to the Lord, and to sing to your name, O Most High; to show forth your mercy in the morning, and your truth in the night.'
It is sung of blessed Dominic: 'traversing by night the thresholds of heaven, he gave to the earth the seeds of the word.'

Twenty-fifth, as the same author says, in the same place, fish come more readily to new vessels by which they are caught than to old ones; indeed, unless a vessel is new, they do not easily approach it.

It signifies the curious in knowledge, who always seek and run after new sayings or writings, and abandon, 2 Timothy, the ancient and perfect sciences: 'for there shall be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but, according to their own desires, will heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; and will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth, but will be turned to fables.'
Augustine: 'the knowledge of certain philosophers, while it delights, is opposed to the Gospel.'
Twenty-sixth, as Aristotle says, book 7, fish are universally gluttonous and greedy, and for the most part eat flesh if they have it.
They signify those given to gluttony and voraciousness and pleasure, Philippians 3: 'whose god is their belly.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'The pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers.'
Fish lay their eggs among birds and fish.
It signifies that subjects are dissolved and released from discipline in the absence of a prelate, and are sometimes spiritually devoured by demons.
...the molten calf.
Twenty-eighth, as the same Aristotle says, in the same place, at the time of mating the males and females of fish wander like a flock and go about, each paired with its mate.

They signify the lustful and the wanton, going about together and pleasing themselves in the desires of the flesh, Wisdom 2: 'let us everywhere leave tokens of joy. Let no meadow escape our riot. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither.'

Jerome, on Paul: 'a belly seething with wine easily boils over into lust. He who lives in luxury is dead while he lives; lust tames even iron minds, a lust that suffers a greater hunger among virgins, the more sweetly they think of all that they do not know. Oh, how bitter the fruit of luxury, more bitter than gall, more cruel than the sword.'
Twenty-ninth, as the same Aristotle says, in the same place, many of them, when they breed, fall ill, and are then most easily caught.

They signify certain men who, glorying in their good works, fall sick in their character and their affections, and so lie easily open to the assaults of lurking demons; against which: 'for what have you that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it?'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Bernard, on the Song of Songs: 'we praise falsely and are delighted in vain. O vanity of vanities! But not more vain than mad.'
Thirtieth, as the same Aristotle says, in the same place, river and marsh fish lay eggs more, and sooner, than others, since for the most part after five months, while others breed only after a year.
They signify that the wicked breed more than the good, and sooner, Ecclesiastes 1: 'the number of fools is infinite.'

Ambrose, in the Hexameron: 'malice comes from us, not established by the Creator; it is generated by levity of character, having no prerogative of creation, nor authority of natural substance, but is a vice of mutability and an error of falling away.'
Thirty-first, as the same Aristotle says, fish suffer when they rub their belly against the sand.

They signify that those who cling too much to the world, and hold fast to it, fall into sin, James 4: 'the friendship of this world is the enemy of God. Whosoever, therefore, will be a friend of this world, becomes an enemy of God.'

Augustine, in the book of the Confessions: 'the friendship of this world, O Lord, is fornication away from you, and "well done, well done" is said, that one may be ashamed if he is not so, though a mere man.'
Thirty-second, as Avicenna says, book 2, chapter 7, the sea-fish that are most praiseworthy are those that are delicate, such as soles and the like.

They signify that those are the better men in the Church, or in religion, who are more perceptive in contemplation and sharper in penetrating and grasping the understanding of holy Scripture, Wisdom 7: 'for in her is a spirit of understanding, manifold, one, subtle. And through nations she conveys herself into holy souls, and makes friends of God and prophets.'

It is written of blessed Francis that 'the untiring zeal of prayer, together with the continual exercise of the virtues, had brought the man of God to such serenity of mind that, although he had no learning of the sacred letters through instruction, yet, illumined by the radiance of eternal light, he scrutinized the depths of the Scriptures with a wondrous sharpness of understanding. For his understanding, pure of every stain, penetrated the hidden things of the mysteries; and where the learning of masters remains outside, the affection of one who loves entered in.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Thirty-third, as Isidore says, book 12, the kinds of fish vary as to food and color and shape, size and quality, length and breadth, shortness and fleshiness, flavor and tastelessness, fragrance and stench, health and sickness, hardness and softness, solidity and looseness.

They signify the varieties, or diversities, of the states of the good and the wicked in the present age, Psalm 103: 'so is this great sea, which stretches wide its arms: there are creeping things without number. Creatures little and great,' and so on.

An example is found in Matthew 13, in the parable of the net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind; where it is added that the good were chosen into vessels, but the bad were cast out beyond the nets and the vessels.
Thirty-fourth, as Aristotle says, large fish breed in the breadth and depth of the waters; but small ones breed in places where the water is shallow, near the roots of trees and reeds.

It signifies that proud and worldly men walk in marvels above themselves, but the poor and humble reduce themselves to small things, and are content with their own limits; wherefore the apostle said, 1 Corinthians 4: 'you are honorable, but we without honor; we are weak, but you are strong. We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are wise in Christ.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'Glorious is humility, with which even pride itself desires to cloak itself, lest it seem base.'
Thirty-fifth, as the same Aristotle says, fish love their young very much, and nourish them for a long time.

They signify that prelates ought to love their subjects, cherish them, and instruct them, with perseverance, 2 Corinthians 11: 'my daily instance, the solicitude for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'those deserve, above all others, to see lofty things, who know how to preside carefully over the faithful. And while they themselves watch piously over the flock, the grace from above shines the more abundantly upon them.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: 144 kinds of fish are found, counting all that live in the waters and take their origin from the waters, but birds are not included in this number.

It signifies the family of the Lamb, Jesus Christ, mystically established in that same number, Revelation 14: 'I saw the Lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him a hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name, and the name of his Father, written on their foreheads.'

bibl.author: Hrabanus Maurus In honorem sancte crucis Hrabani Mauri

cit.quote: Rabanus, in the treatise On the Cross: 'this number, divided into four parts, belongs to the family of the Lamb, shining forth from every arm of the cross.'
Thirty-seventh, as Aristotle says, book 7, no kind of fish has testicles.
It signifies those who are made eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, according to that saying, Matthew 19.
Jerome, to Eustochium: 'for fear of gehenna, I had made myself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX
Basilius Cesariensis Homilie in Hexameron Basilii Cesariensis

cit.quote: In the first place, as Isidore says, book 12, and likewise Basil and Ambrose in the Hexameron, there is found in the sea a certain fish called the whale, or 'balena,' of such great size that it is likened to mountains, from its sending forth, or pouring out, powerful waters over ships so as to overwhelm them, and other things; and it is so named for this reason. For it throws up waves higher than all other sea-monsters. For it is said to be called 'balena' from emitting, or spouting; but 'cetus' is said from the vastness of its body.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: This fish, dwelling in seas most remote from land and unsailed, according to Basil, as is found in the book of Iorath, abounds in seed, and, after its mating with the female, that which remains floats upon the water. This, gathered and collected and dried, is changed into the substance of ambergris. But when it hungers greatly, it sends forth from itself, through its mouth, a certain fragrant vapor in the manner of ambergris, in which fish delight, and, on account of the sweetness of the vapor, they enter into its very mouth, and, thus deceived, are devoured by it.

In all these things it signifies the devil, and the monstrousness of his swelling pride and that of his followers. It signifies also the excessive lust of his members, as under the appearance of the fruit that comes of it, and of a fame published and worked among the world. It signifies, no less, the snares and malice of himself and his followers, which, under the pretext of love and offered consolation, allure and draw souls deceitfully, and in the end devour them.
'But in the end he shall be shamefully confounded, and Leviathan the ancient serpent, and upon Leviathan the crooked serpent, and he shall slay the whale that is in the sea.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'the ancient enemy is said to be wrapped in bitterness, since punishments for his pride and wickedness are prepared, not only of every kind, but also without end.'
'Your pride is brought down to hell, your carcass has fallen.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: As is likewise found in Iorath, On Animals, in this fish earthy matter prevails more than watery, and therefore it is of great corpulence and fatness. Whence, in old age, on account of the greatness of its body, dust gathers and thickens upon its back to such a degree that grasses and shrubs grow there, so that the beast appears like an island, to which, if sailors carelessly draw near, they scarcely escape without danger, because of the water it spouts from its mouth. It is also of such fatness that, when it is struck by the harpoons or spears of fishermen, it feels no wound until the fat is entirely pierced through. But when the inner flesh is wounded, then it is most easily taken. It is, moreover, of such size that, when it is caught, the whole surrounding country is filled and made abundant by its capture.

In these things it signifies the great lovers of earthly things who, filled with worldly goods and the sproutings of many sins, are dangerous to their neighbors and to strangers, and are scarcely pierced by the goads of divine love or by the words of holy preaching. Yet, sometimes, once pierced and converted to God, they fill the whole surrounding country with edification, and spiritually console it.

An example is found, Acts 13, in Sergius the proconsul, a man prudent according to the world, who, converted by the preaching of Paul, built up so much that he filled the whole Church with consolation; he also so greatly delighted Paul that, out of love for the conversion of such and so great a man, when he had been called Saul, he chose to be called Paul, as blessed Augustine writes in the book of the Confessions.

Augustine likewise gives another example, in the book of the Confessions, of Victorinus, the rhetorician of the city of Rome, converted in a similar way, with the whole Church rejoicing, and every Christian soul flowering again.

This same whale loves its young with a wondrous love, and leads them about in the deep sea for a long time. But if they should happen to be hindered by heaps of sand, it pours over them the great quantity of water gathered in its mouth, and so, freeing them from danger, calls and leads them back to the depth of the sea. Against every harmful encounter it places itself in their defense, and always sets them between itself and the sea, on the safer side. And when a storm grows strong, it draws its offspring, still young and tender, into its own belly, and, once the calm has come, brings them forth alive again, and sends them out.

It signifies the solicitude and tender love that prelates ought to have for instructing and cherishing their subjects in Christ, and protecting them from every danger: 'the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.'
'We became little ones in the midst of you, as if a nurse should cherish her children,' and so on.

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: 'He who presides over others in solicitude scarcely, or rarely, ever has leisure for himself, since he always fears God, in that he prefers the common good to his own sweet quiet of contemplation.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: The same Iorath also writes that a certain serpentine and venomous fish fights against the whale, like the crocodile, and fish flee to the tail of the whale, which, if it is defeated, causes the aforesaid fish to die. But if that pestilent fish cannot defeat the whale, it sends from its jaws a smoky, most foul-smelling odor into the waters; the whale, however, drives away the foul smell with a fragrant smoke sent from its mouth, and so protects and defends itself and its own.

They signify the battle of the just against demons and sins, and the teaching of heretics and the teaching of catholics, and its effect, Ecclesiasticus 4: 'strive for justice for your soul, and contend even unto death for justice, and God will fight for you against your enemies. Be not ashamed to speak the truth for your soul; for there is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory and grace.'

In the tenth book of the Ecclesiastical History: when the holy fathers had gathered at the Council of Nicaea, and philosophers and dialecticians had also been present there, one philosopher stirred up, to the peril of the faith, a dispute against the bishops, so forcefully that it became a great spectacle, and none of the fathers could refute him. Seeing this, one of the confessors, a simple man, knowing nothing at all but Jesus Christ, and him crucified, asked to be allowed to speak with the philosopher. Hearing this, and knowing his simplicity, they would not permit it, fearing lest the faith be exposed to mockery. But he, wholly resolved to speak for himself, rose and said: 'hear, philosopher, in the name of Jesus Christ, the things that are true. There is one God, who made all things and created them by the power of his Word; this Word and Wisdom, whom we call the Son, was made flesh, and by his passion and death redeemed us from eternal death, and shall return from heaven as judge of all. Do you believe this, philosopher?' And he, struck dumb and astonished at the power of these words, believed, and with him many others; and so they were added to the number of the sacred council.

In the second place there is a certain fish in the sea, the dolphin, which has these conditions, according to Isidore and Ambrose in the Hexameron and Basil. For it follows the voices of sailors, and gathers in schools at the sound of music, and delights wonderfully in harmony. Nothing in the sea is swifter than they, for very often, leaping, they fly over ships, and their leaping and playing among the waves signifies a coming storm. These fish, moreover, have serrated backs, with which, cutting the inner parts of their bellies, they kill crocodiles, those serpentine fish hostile to the whale, as was said above. Being also of a fittingly great size, they are of much use as food for man.
This fish suckles its young, small as they are, as Aristotle says, book 6.

They signify contemplative men and true religious who, hearing and perceiving and following the voices, or inspirations, of angels and of the Gospels, out of affection lift up their supermental ears to the harmonies of heaven, and delight supremely in perceiving them, and find themselves ever more ready to lift their actions upward toward God, leaving worldly things behind and seeking things beyond the world, and, amid the waves of temptations or tribulations, rejoicing and glorying after the manner of the apostles, and not keeping silent about the eternal calamity to come upon the world and those who follow it, and, with the vehemence and sharpness of zeal, casting down and cutting apart heretics and adversaries of the faith and other pestilent sinners; and thus, wholly benefiting the universal Church, singularly nourishing its weak members in Christ.

An example is found in the apostle Paul, to whom all these things actually happened from the time of his conversion, and were found in him, as is universally clear from the Acts of the Apostles and from his own letters.
An example is also found in Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, and Gregory, and many like them, as is clear from the course of their life and teaching, and is plain to the wise.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: In the third place, that fish called the 'southern fish' has these conditions, according to Isidore and Iorath. For fish of this kind are born when the stars of the Pleiades begin to set, nor do they appear until the Pleiades rise again.

They signify those who conceive a holy purpose from the consideration, and for the sake of considering, the examples of the holy fathers or martyrs who died for Christ, and who spring forth publicly in holy works, for the instruction and example of modern saints, or good religious, after the likeness of the Pleiades, shining uniformly in life and teaching, and running about, out of charity, for offices of piety, James: 'take, my brethren, for an example, the prophets,' and so on.

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: Seneca, in a letter: 'men trust their eyes more than their ears; for the way by precepts is long, but by examples short and effective.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the fourth place, that fish called 'ephemeron' is of this condition, according to Iorath in the book On Animals. For it is born without mating, and when it has lived through three hours of the day, then it dies.

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: It signifies sin, which indeed has no cause but a deficient one, according to Dionysius and the Philosopher, and comes to be, or lasts, only for a short time; 'but the having done it remains forever,' according to Bernard, On Consideration, James 1: 'when desire has conceived, it brings forth sin; but sin, when it is completed, begets death.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis Tractatus Augustini in Iohannis Evangelium

cit.quote: Augustine, on John: 'sin is nothing, and men become nothing when they sin.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the fifth place, that fish called 'faste' is of this condition, according to what Iorath says in the book On Animals. For water drawn into its mouth becomes sweet, and smaller fish, sensing this and following it, enter its mouth, which it then suddenly takes and swallows.
...souls.

bibl.author: Prosper Aquitanus Liber sententiarum ex operibus sancti Augustini

cit.quote: Augustine, in the Sentences of Prosper: 'the tongues of flatterers bind souls fast in sins.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the sixth place, that astonishing fish called the sea-urchin, or remora, is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12, and Ambrose in the Hexameron. For it is small, scarcely half a foot, and is named from clinging. For although it is of tiny body, yet it is of the greatest power. For, by clinging, it holds a ship fast, and, once it has attached itself, though the winds rush and storms rage, the ship seems to stand as though rooted in the sea, and does not move. And this it does, not by restraining, but only by clinging. The Latins called it 'mora' (delay), because it compels ships to be delayed, or to stand still, as is found in the same place.

bibl.author: Basilius Cesariensis Homilie in Hexameron Basilii Cesariensis

cit.quote: Likewise Basil writes, in the Hexameron, book 8, chapter 6, and blessed Ambrose likewise in the Hexameron, and Bede, that this fish, foreseeing the coming storm of the winds, seizes a strong pebble and, as it were an anchor, so as not to be shaken off by the waves, drags it, or places it upon its back, and does not free itself by its own strength, but is fortified by another's weight, and made steady against the storms to come. Seeing this, sailors take precautions for themselves, lest the storm overtake them unforeseen.

In its first condition, or property, it gives men occasion to consider and to know plainly how great is the power of the Creator in its source, or origin, when so much is found in the effect of so small a creature of his. Likewise, by this same thing, is signified to us the virtue of humility, how great it is, since it accomplishes the greatest things.

It drew the almighty Son of God into her womb, and set him over heaven and earth, and made him singularly worthy of regard, just as she herself says, Luke 1: 'he has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from this all generations shall call me blessed.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Ambrose, on Luke: 'nothing is loftier than humility.' 'Humility alone deserves glory.'

But in its second condition, or property, it gives to, and impresses upon, penitent men caution and circumspection and forewarning against the coming judgment or death, or even against imminent dangers, or temptations and adversities, so that, that is, they may receive, above the mind and in their affections, Christ, the cornerstone, founding and steadying and joining, or fitting together, bodies and souls, preserving them to God and protecting them from every danger, at every hour and place: 'coming to whom, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen and honored by God; be you also, as living stones, built up into spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.'
This the apostles and disciples in the primitive Church duly carried into effect, as is found fully in the Acts and in the Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the 'aphorus' is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so small that it cannot be caught by a hook, and so hooks do no harm to it.

It signifies that the snares of the devil's temptations cannot harm the truly humble, Ecclesiasticus 13: 'humble yourself to God, and wait for his hands' — that is, the help of the effects of his power and goodness. An example is told by blessed Jerome, in the Lives of the Fathers, that blessed Anthony saw the whole world full of snares, and, wishing to know who could escape them, heard by revelation that humility alone could.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the moray eel is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12, and blessed Ambrose in the Hexameron. For it does not conceive, or is conceived, from one like itself, but from a serpent, which the serpent, by hissing, invites to its embraces, taking its stand beside the shore. The Greeks call it 'sinnina,' since it coils itself into circles. They relate that it is of the female sex, and conceives from the serpent, as has been said. For this reason it is called and caught by fishermen with a hiss. Struck with a club, it is scarcely killed; but with a rod, at once. It is certain that it has its life in its tail; for, struck on the head, they say it is scarcely killed, but, its tail struck and cut off, it is said to die at once. With the serpent it is the reverse; for, its head crushed or cut off, it dies at once, but, its tail cut off, it lives a long time. They also say that the serpent lays aside its venom before it mates with the moray eel, but, once the act of generation is complete, takes back its venom. And so the moray eel contracts no venom from the serpent, nor does it beget anything like the serpent, but only something like itself.

These things signify the suggestions of the devil toward souls, and about subjecting to himself souls both unsubjected and already subjected. They signify, no less, those who can endure much for the world and nothing for God. They signify also those who relapse into a sin once given up. They signify, too, those who do not have their souls where they ought, that is, lifted up to heavenly things, but bent down toward earthly ones: 'they said to your soul: bow down, that we may pass over; and you have made your body as the earth, and as a way for them that walk over it.'
'The dog is returned to his vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.' An example is found in Julian the Apostate and many others like him.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the ninth place, the fish called oysters, or shellfish, or mollusks, are of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12, chapter 6. For they conceive from dew alone, without eggs or seed. For by night they come out of the water and, on land, conceive and give birth from the morning dew. Their shells, moreover, always remain empty during the waning of the moon.

But in these fish precious pearls are generated, as Pliny states, and others who have written on the natures of living things, since, at nighttime, they make for the shores and conceive pearls from the heavenly dew. Whence such shellfish are called pearl-bearing and beryl-like, in whose flesh a precious stone is formed, and is a most noble gem, generated thus from the dew of the springtime, which, the whiter and more lustrous it is, is esteemed the more precious. There are also certain shellfish, or thorny shells, called from their roughness and sharpness, which by another name are called 'purple-fish,' which, cut around with iron, emit tears of purple color, from which purple dye is made.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: And from this the purple dye is called 'ostrum,' since this coloring is drawn out from the moisture of the shell, as Isidore says, in the book and chapter cited above.

They signify blessed Mary and her virgins, and likewise other saints, who, fleeing the world's lusts, exposed and fitted themselves to holy desires and to heavenly influences, and conceived within themselves, spiritually, Christ Jesus, the precious evangelical pearl and most noble gem, and brought forth works of angelic chastity and apostolic sanctity, the more precious the more they shone before God and men, and were full of every kind of edification. Some of these women, and some of these men, shed and poured out their blood by the iron of martyrdom for the name of Christ, and by this means adorned the whole Church, and decked it as with royal purple.

And these are the things that the eternal bridegroom, Christ, requires of every such person conformed and devoted to him, Song of Songs 5: 'the voice of my beloved knocking: open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled, for my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De trinitate Augustini Hipponensis

cit.quote: Augustine, in the book On the Trinity, in the person of a soul devoted to Christ: 'where you have opened to me, receive me as I enter; where you have closed, open to me as I knock. May I remember you, understand you, love you; increase these things in me, until you reform me wholly.'
For this I marvel at the power of God; for this I marvel at the ready spirit of Paul, since he strove to show himself such, and prepared himself to be capable of so great a grace.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the mullet, or 'cephalus,' is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12: 'the mullet,' he says, 'is a very agile kind of fish; for as soon as it senses the snares set by fishermen, it at once retreats backward, and so swiftly leaps over the net, that it seems to have flown, to the fishermen and those standing by.'

It signifies, spiritually, those who are shrewd, keen, and cunning in escaping the temptations of the devil and the snares of his ambushes, 1 Peter 5: 'be sober and watch, for your adversary the devil,' and so on.
...of Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices.
Ambrose, On Abel and Cain: 'the testimony of heavenly begetting is victory over temptation.'
An example is found in blessed Benedict who, feeling a temptation of lust, overcame it by casting himself into stinging briars, as Gregory says in the second book of the Dialogues.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the parrotfish is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12, and Pliny. For it alone among fish is said to chew the cud, having something like food already taken, and so it is thus named. It is, moreover, very ingenious, for when it senses that it has entered the fisherman's basket, it does not burst out headfirst, nor thrust its head between the woven withies, but by repeated strokes of its tail against the opening it begins to loosen it, and so returns backward. And if, by chance, another parrotfish should see it struggling from outside, to help it in its effort to break free, it grasps its tail in its mouth as best it can, and strives to free and draw it out.

It signifies that man ought to have caution in escaping the snares of his neighbors, and the good fellowship, or help, of the saints for this very purpose, Ecclesiasticus 9: 'according to your power, beware of your neighbor.'
'A brother that is helped by his brother is like a strong city.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis Epistola Augustini ad Probam

cit.quote: 'May good men be present, whatever sad things may be lightened.'

bibl.author: Basilius Cesariensis Homilie in Hexameron Basilii Cesariensis

cit.quote: That fish called the conger eel, or octopus, is of this condition, according to Isidore and Pliny and Basil in the Hexameron. For, having many feet and many joints, it is very ingenious in the skill of acquiring food. For, desiring the bait on a hook, but fearing and being wary of the barb, it embraces the hook not with a bite but with its little fins, and does not let it go until it has gnawed all around the bait.

The octopus is, moreover, of such great cunning, deceitful and thieving, as Basil says, that when it embraces a rock with its outstretched tentacles, it takes on that rock's color, and many fish, unwittingly gliding there, and simply drawing near as if to a plain rock, are easily deceived, and at once offer themselves to be caught by the malicious octopus.

bibl.author: Basilius Cesariensis Homilie in Hexameron Basilii Cesariensis

cit.quote: According to the same Basil, it signifies those who, 'most skillful about worldly gains, are changed by the fickleness of their mind, and, not persevering in one purpose, show themselves now one thing, now another, practicing modesty with the chaste, wantonness with the wanton, and altogether fitting their own character to whatever anyone else's mind happens to be. These men, too, it is difficult to avoid, on account of the wickedness that lies hidden in their pretense; men of this kind the Lord called ravening wolves, Matthew 7, feigning themselves simple sheep.' Thus far Basil, in the Hexameron.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the thirteenth place, crabs are of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For, having claws and stings, they are hostile to oysters or shellfish, and live on their flesh, by an admirable cunning. For, since they cannot open their strong and hard shell, they watch for when the oysters, at night, open the closed shells to the dew, and then, lurking in ambush, they cast in a small stone, so that the oyster cannot afterward close its shell, and so, its closing hindered, the crab devours and gnaws away the oyster's flesh.

They signify the devil and wicked men who sometimes overcome, by cunning, those they cannot overcome by power. Likewise, that demons and heretics, under the appearance of what is right, gladly introduce errors and sins into consciences: 'for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. It is no wonder, then, if his ministers also transform themselves as the ministers of justice, whose end shall be according to their works.'

Blessed Jerome, in the Lives of the Fathers, gives an example of two philosophers who came to tempt blessed Anthony, and, by magic art, sent demons to drive him from the wilderness; yet neither these philosophers nor these demons could prevail against him, by cunning or by power, since he dwelt in the help of the Most High.

In the fourteenth place, the fish called the crawfish is of this condition, according to Aristotle, book 6. 'The crawfish,' he says, 'overcomes large fish and eats them; but the octopus overcomes the crawfish and eats it.'
Likewise, in the same place, the same author states that the crawfish feeds in mud and slime, and is for this reason heavy, and much mud is found within it.

As to the first condition, it signifies those who, holding power in this world, oppress those beneath them, and are at last oppressed, by divine judgment, by one lower than themselves. An example is found in Haman, Esther 2, 3, and 4, who, holding power, oppressed Mordecai and his people, and at last, by the arrangement of that same Mordecai, less powerful than he, through the ministry of the woman Esther, was hanged upon the gallows.
An example is also found in Holofernes, Judith 12, who, wishing to oppress an entire leading nation, was nonetheless beheaded by a single woman.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the fifteenth place, that fish called the dentex is of this condition, as Isidore says, book 12. For it has very strong teeth, so much so that it is nourished on oysters in the sea, whence it is called 'dentix,' for the size and strength and multitude of its teeth.

It signifies the devil, who is of such recklessness and such manifold violent and sharp temptations, that he sometimes assails not only subjects or the weak, but even prelates and the perfect, and the most steadfast in faith, and feeds on their ruin: 'he will swallow up a river, and not wonder; he trusts that the Jordan may run into his mouth. In his eyes as it were with a hook he shall take him, and bore through his nose with pierces. Round about his teeth is terror. His flesh sticks together. Out of his nostrils goes forth smoke. His breath kindles coals.'

Cassian gives an example, in the Conferences, of a man of God for fifty years, whom the devil at last brought to ruin, tempting him and showing him that he had attained to such a grace that a fall from a height could not harm him; he cast himself into a well, and died.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the sixteenth place, that fish called the sea-hog is, by consideration or rather by condition, as Isidore says, book 12. For, after the manner of the land-hog, it seeks food by digging the earth under the waters; for it has its mouth-opening near its throat, and unless it thrusts its snout into the sand, it does not gather its food.

It signifies the greedy and the gluttonous, 2 Peter 2: 'having eyes full of adultery, and of sin that ceases not; having a heart exercised with covetousness, esteeming as a pleasure the delights of a day.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: 'The pleasure of gluttony, so highly esteemed today, occupies scarcely the breadth of two fingers.'
That fish called the 'fastaleon' is of this condition, according to Aristotle, book 7. For, with this exception, fish for the most part eat flesh, and, at the time of their breeding, eat one another.

It signifies a holy man, austere to himself, while others devote themselves to their flesh, and, for this reason, even seize what belongs to others, Galatians 5: 'and they that are Christ's have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences. Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which I have foretold you, as I have also foretold you, that they who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God.'
Pope Leo, in the sermon On Palm Sunday, speaking of the Jewish people and the suffering Christ: 'you shall abound in delights, but he drank vinegar and gall.'

Eighteenth, that fish called the 'abatue' is of this condition, according to Aristotle, book 7. For while other fish are gluttonous and greedy by nature, this one is so especially, and by excess; and for this reason its belly is distended. When it is fasting it is bad-tempered, and often swells its belly and casts out other fish from itself, since its belly reaches all the way to its mouth, and it has no stomach.

It signifies those who serve only their own belly, and labor for nothing else. And when they do not have their fill, they murmur, and bear themselves impatiently, and then fight and rail. But when they do have it, they eat so much that they cast out again what they have eaten.

An example is found in the children of Israel, Numbers 11, who, taken by excessive gluttony, murmured because they did not have what they wanted, and, once they had it, ate so much that the food came out through their nostrils, upon whom the wrath of God came, by divine judgment: 'meat for the belly, and the belly for meats; but God shall destroy both it and them.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Gregory, in the Moralia: 'when the belly is not restrained from the lust of the flesh, all the virtues together are overwhelmed; whence also the chiefs of the cooks destroyed Jerusalem.'
Jerome, on the letter to the Ephesians, and in his letters: 'a belly seething with wine quickly boils over into lust.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the nineteenth place, that fish called the gilthead is of this condition. For, as Isidore says, book 12, it is called 'aurata' (golden) from its color, since it has the color of gold on its head. This fish is precious, not only in color, but also in flavor and value, according to experience.

It signifies those who are precious to the Church everywhere, in the gold of wisdom, in mind and conduct and teaching: 'the multitude of the wise is the health of the whole world.' An example is found in Paul and Augustine and the like.
Would anyone call Paul's soul golden, or rather adamantine?
For it was stronger than any adamant, and more precious than any gold and gems: Proverbs 3, 'wisdom is more precious than all things.'

But as to the second condition, it signifies those who always lie in luxury, and whose feeding is wantonness together with filth, and who, being wholly and entirely bowed down toward earthly things, can never savor heavenly ones: 'I stick fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no sure standing.'
'The movement of pleasure, being greatest, is likewise most hostile to philosophy; for bodily delight cannot agree with understanding.'

bibl.author: Augustinus Hipponensis De spiritu et anima Alcheri Clarevallensis

cit.quote: The same, On the Spirit and the Soul: 'bodily delight hinders the knowledge of spiritual good.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Those river fish of upper Italy, commonly called 'temeri,' are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, existing in a twofold kind, one kind feeds chiefly on gold, which it seeks and picks out from the sand for itself, and has a golden color for this reason. The other kind feeds on silver, which it seeks and picks out from the sand in like manner, and has a silvery color for a like reason. This fish, twofold in each of its kinds, is choice, precious, equally flavorful, and both beautiful and pleasing.

The golden fish signify the wise who savor heavenly things in their hearts; the silver ones signify those eloquent in speech in evangelical teaching, Proverbs 20: 'gold, and a multitude of jewels, and a precious vessel, are the lips of knowledge.'
'My fruit is better than gold and precious stones, and my offspring than choice silver.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: By the name of gold is understood the preciousness of wisdom; by silver is designated sacred eloquence, whence: 'the words of the Lord are silver,' and so on.

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: For this reason Seneca says, in letter 94, that the times when the wise ruled were called the golden times, and the golden ages.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus

cit.quote: The fish called 'elyth' are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For by night they come out of the water, and, on land, conceive and give birth from the morning dew, whose shells, like those of oysters, always remain empty during the waning of the moon.

They signify those who conceive holy desires and saving purposes, and perform good works from a heavenly influence to which they expose and dispose themselves, and, once it withdraws, they are shown to themselves as they truly are: 'draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.'
'They who watch for me early shall find me. All they that hate me love death.'
An example is found in Paul and blessed Augustine and the like, who drew near to the feet of Christ, and received from his teaching, as is found in Deuteronomy 33.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the twenty-second place, that fish called the trout is of this condition. For, as Isidore says, book 12, trout are variable in color, as experience also shows. This fish is precious, and flavorful, and pleasing.

It signifies a cleric or a religious man shining before his neighbors, preciously and with edification, discretion, and grace, in the variety of his sacred habits and deeds: 'as a solid vessel of gold, adorned with every precious stone.'

In this mystery is found, Wisdom 18: 'for in the priestly robe which he wore was the whole world; and in the four rows of stones were the great deeds of the fathers.' It is written of blessed Dominic that he abounded with such honesty of character, and was carried, in all things, by such an impulse of divine fervor, that no one who observed him carefully could doubt that he was a vessel of honor and of grace, a vessel adorned with every precious stone. Something similar is read and sung of blessed Bernard.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: The fish called sea-wolves, or 'spilulae,' are of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For they are as voracious in the waters as wolves are on land. For they pursue others shamelessly, and devour whatever they can.

bibl.author: Epistola Pauli ad Thessalonicenses prima Apostolus

cit.quote: ...robbers and oppressors of other men, certainly to be judged in the end, according to the pattern of the Apostle, 1 Thessalonians 4: 'and that no man overreach, nor circumvent his brother in business, because the Lord is the avenger of all these things,' and so on.
Isaiah 33: 'woe to you who plunder; shall you not yourself also be plundered?'
We have an example in Julian the Apostate, and in the emperor Decius, and in very many others, in the Tripartite History.
This fish is cunning in escaping capture; indeed, surrounded by a net, it is said to plow the sand with its tail, and so, roused, to pass through the net.

It signifies those who are shrewd in escaping the snares and temptations of demons, by the way of evangelical humility and holy prayer, 1 Corinthians 7: 'give yourselves to prayer, lest Satan tempt you.'
'Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation.'

...of the holy father Anthony, who could not be assailed by demons, because he was always found praying or reading, weeping or signing himself with the cross, as blessed Jerome relates in the book of the Lives of the Fathers.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the twenty-fourth place, that fish called the 'orbis' (globe-fish) is of this condition. For, as Isidore says, book 12, it is so named from its shape. For it is round, and consists entirely of its head.
It signifies a man expanded by wholehearted charity, rooted in Christ his head, 2 Corinthians 6: 'our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged.'
Ambrose, in the Gloss on 2 Kings, chapter 1: 'if you rejoice in Jesus, your heart is enlarged.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the sole, as Isidore says, book 12, is so named because it resembles the sole of a shoe in shape. Likewise, as experience shows, it is delicate and has firm flesh.
'Seek the Lord in goodness and simplicity of heart, for he is found by those who do not tempt him, but appears to those who have faith in him.'

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam Ambrosii

cit.quote: Against which, Ambrose, on Luke: 'those who are occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the twenty-sixth place, those fish called the ravens are of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For they are called 'ravens' from the voice of their heart, since they grunt from the breast, and, betrayed by their own voice, are caught.
They signify those who, unwary in their bodily senses, betray themselves to demons and to men, whereby they are apprehended in their vices, Proverbs 11: 'the sinner is caught in his own vanity.'
Ecclesiasticus 19: 'the attire of the body, and the laughter of the teeth, and the gait of the man, show what he is.'

Blessed Jerome tells an example, in the book of the Lives of the Fathers, of a certain father who, watching those entering the church, could even know the thoughts of those entering by their very faces. He saw one entering black on account of sin, and coming out bright on account of the merit of contrition, and praised, out of affection, the eternal and good God.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: Those fish called tunnies are of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For, when they enter in springtime, they enter on the right side, and go out on the left. This is believed to be because they see more sharply with the right eye than with the left.

They signify those who, grace smiling upon them, enter into the Church, or into religion, with a heavenly purpose, and afterward apostatize at the devil's instigation; who nevertheless saw more sharply and better upon entering than they see upon leaving, Galatians 3: 'are you so foolish, that, whereas you began in the Spirit, you now are made perfect by the flesh?'

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: Such were Julian the Apostate and Torquatus, the familiar of Tiburtius, and many others, of whom is found in the Tripartite and Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the swordfish is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so named because, armed with a great beak, it thereby pierces and sinks ships.

It signifies the devil, armed with the sting of temptations, endangering souls by his assaults, Revelation 12: 'the serpent cast out of his mouth, after the woman, water as it were a flood, that he might cause her to be carried away by the flood.'

bibl.author: Iohannes Damascenus De fide orthodoxa Iohannis Damasceni

cit.quote: Damascene, in his little book: 'all malice and all impurity were devised by the devil.'
Wherefore, Jeremiah 50, he is called the hammer of the whole earth.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the sawfish is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so named because 'it has a serrated crest, and, swimming beneath, cuts the ship.'

It signifies heretics, brazen of face and barbed or serrated of tongue, who, deceitfully creeping in among those who walk simply, cut open their souls and ferment them, and so endanger them, 1 Corinthians 15: 'evil communications corrupt good manners.'
...spreads like a cancer. Among these are Philetus and Hymenaeus, who have fallen away from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and have overturned the faith of some.
Of Nicholas, the newcomer from Antioch, and Muhammad, and Julian the Apostate, and the like, of whom is found in the Ecclesiastical and Tripartite History.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the thirtieth place, that fish called the scorpion-fish is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so called 'because it harms when it is taken up by hand.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: It is related of this fish, as the same Isidore says in the same place, that all fish of its kind in a district gather at the spot where ten crabs have been bound together in a bundle in the water.

They signify impatient men, or even hypocrites and detractors, who, when they are touched by the truth, recoil and sting, and gladly, wherever they are, apostates or even heretics or other wicked men make their leader: 'the body of Behemoth,' that is, of the devil, that is, all the wicked, 'like molten shields, joined together with scales pressing one upon another; one is joined to another,' and so on.

bibl.author: Seneca Lucius Anneus Epistole Senece ad Lucilium

cit.quote: Against which, Seneca, to Lucilius: 'the first step to innocence is to hate wicked things.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the thirty-first place, that fish called the weever, or spider-fish, is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so named because it has stings with which it strikes.

It signifies quarrelsome, or abusive men, in matters of faith; against which, 2 Timothy 2: 'contend not in words, for it is to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers. For it spreads much toward ungodliness; and their speech creeps like a cancer.'

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis De viris illustribus Hieronymi

cit.quote: Such were Cerinthus and Marcion, as Jerome says in the book On Illustrious Men.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the thirty-second place, that fish called the crocodile is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so named 'from its saffron color. It is born in the Nile, a four-footed animal, strong both on land and in the waters, generally of a length of twenty cubits, armed with the vastness of its teeth and claws, and of such hardness of skin that, although struck on the back with the blow of strong stones, it does not feel it. By night it rests in the waters, by day on the ground.' It lays eggs on land; the male and female take turns keeping watch; certain fish, having a serrated crest, kill it by cutting the tender parts of its belly. It alone among animals is said to move its upper jaw.

It signifies a religious and perfect man, gracious in life and character, wisely generated in the river of holy Scripture, planted together with the four cardinal virtues in his affections and acts, universally armed in mind and speech with magnanimity and zeal, made unshakably and perseveringly steadfast, by constancy and equanimity, against hostile assaults, devoting himself by night to prayer and devotion, by day to the edification of the weak. He is also singularly refreshed, as if from above, by the food of heavenly consolation, and carries others along toward it. Yet sometimes heretics or tyrants, exposing him to the stings of pride, inflict torments where he is tender and fragile, that is, upon the body only — namely, death.

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De divinis nominibus Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Such in every way was the apostle Paul, as his letters testify, when he answered point by point, and as Chrysostom proves in many ways, in On the Praises of Paul, and as blessed Dionysius writes to his fellow disciple Timothy.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the thirty-third place, that fish called the hippopotamus is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so named 'because it is like a horse in its back, mane, and neighing, with a snout turned up, boar-like tusks, a twisting tail, and cloven hooves; by day it stays in the water, by night it grazes the crops; the Nile produces it.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: It signifies the evangelical preacher, likened to a horse, according to Gregory, on that saying of Job 29: 'will you give strength to the horse, or clothe his neck with neighing?'

This evangelical preacher, in the manner of this fish which bears a likeness to the horse, ought to have a back of willing subjection, a mane of the manifold desires of the homeland, a neighing of evangelical proclamation, a snout turned up from its first teeth through the austerity of sacred abstinence, a twisting tail through the caution of perseverance, cloven hooves through a twofold zeal of twinned charity, that is, of life and doctrine; by day he ought to dwell in the waters, that is, among the peoples to be built up, by night he ought to be refreshed by contemplation, and, no less, be born wisely and nourished in the Nile of holy Scripture, so as to be able to accomplish all that has been said. All these things are found to have been in the apostle Peter, as is clear from the Acts of the Apostles, and is very fully found in the Itinerary.
...of Jerome and Ambrose, as is clear from their deeds.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the sea bream, which the Greeks call 'phagros,' is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For 'it has hard teeth, so that it is nourished on oysters.'

It signifies a religious man such as the venerable Baptist was, endowed with abstinence and austerity of life and teaching, in the vehemence of strong zeal, Matthew 3: 'John himself had his garment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his food was locusts and wild honey.'
Augustine, in the Confessions, speaking of Ambrose: 'only his celibacy seemed a hard thing to me.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the thirty-fifth place, that fish called the sea-hare is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For 'the hare-fish is named from the likeness of its head.'
...the lion of the hare.
...a martyr among the forty martyrs, who, made faint-hearted, fled to the baths, as is found in the Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the thirty-sixth place, that fish called the red mullet is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is called 'mullus, as it were soft, and most tender; they say that eating it restrains lust, but dulls the sharpness of the eyes. Men who often have this fish in their diet, as the same Isidore likewise states in the same place, are said to smell of it; and this fish, drowned in wine, keeps those who drink of it afterward from having a distaste for wine.'

It signifies an evangelical man, gentle, tractable, and kind, whose teaching contends for chastity, refutes worldly prudence, and, by the virtue of abstinence, makes those close to him fragrant and pleasant.

Likewise, dead to the world, by the drunkenness of the love of Christ, he causes others, by his own example, not only to have no distaste for this wine, but to be seized with a burning desire for it, 2 Kings 23: 'he is like the tenderest worm of wood, who slew eight hundred men at one onset.'
Galatians 2: 'I live, now not I,' and so on.

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita De divinis nominibus Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Dionysius, On the Divine Names: 'divine love is ecstatic.'
An example is found in blessed Ambrose who, as is written in the Tripartite History, showed himself, in all things, as has been said above, in the time of Theodosius.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the thirty-seventh place, that fish called the melanurus is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so called because 'it has a black tail and black fins, and black lines on its head; for the Greeks call black "melan."'
It signifies the sinful man, whose mind, desires, character, works, and speech are all darkened, Psalm 81: 'they have walked in darkness; all the foundations of the earth shall be moved.'

Blessed Jerome writes, in the Lives of the Fathers, that a certain holy father saw a certain sinner entering the church wholly black, but coming out wholly bright, on account of the merit of his contrition.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the 'glaucus' is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For 'it is so named from its color, since it is white; for the Greeks call white "glaukon."' This fish rarely appears in summer, except in cloudy weather.

It signifies a man bright with chastity, whose manner of life is not in the heat of any evil desire, but only in piety and devotion, 1 Timothy 4: 'be an example to the faithful, in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, in chastity. Exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise is profitable to little; but godliness is profitable to all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.'
Ambrose, in the Ordinary Gloss, in the same place: 'the sum of the Christian religion consists in godliness,' and so on.

That fish called the grayling is of this condition, according to Isidore. For 'it took its name from a flower; for thyme is indeed called a flower. For, though it is pleasing in appearance and delightful in flavor, it nonetheless is fragrant like a flower, and breathes forth, both in body and in scent.'
It signifies those who are flowering in their desires, gracious in conduct, sweetening others by their learning, famous for their goodness, and eager for eternity.
Such in every way was Paul, as is clear from the course of his letters and from the book On His Praises.
Such was blessed Nicholas, as is clear from his deeds, or legend.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the fortieth place, that fish called the 'sparus' is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For 'it took its name from the throwing-spear, since it has the same shape; for names on land were found before names at sea; for the "sparus" is a rustic missile weapon, named from scattering.'
'Generation of vipers, who has shown you to flee from the wrath to come?'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Homilie in Hiezechielem Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: 'Nothing pleases God so much as zeal for souls.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the forty-first place, that fish called the 'hamio' is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so called 'because it is not caught except by a hook, being marked out among the rocks by its sides, right and left, with continual little reddish streaks, and by wings of varied color.'

It signifies the devil, who could not be caught except by the hook of Christ's cross, though he was hedged in, right and left, as it were by rocks, with his demons and evil men, and irremediably stuffed full of manifold cunning and malice, Job 26: 'his wisdom' — that is, Christ's, on the cross — 'has struck down the proud devil.' Likewise in the same book, chapter 40: 'can you draw out Leviathan,' that is, the devil, 'with a hook, and bind his tongue with a cord?' As though the Lord were saying to Job: 'this neither is, nor will be, except by Christ alone, suffering on the cross.'
Fish, Tobit 6: the devil, standing over the arm of the cross, considered whether Christ had any stain, and, seeing that he had none, knew that he was himself defeated.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the forty-second place, that fish called the 'uranoscopus' (sky-gazer) is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so named from the opening it has on its head, with which it always looks upward.

It signifies a man having a heavenly desire, by means of which he always looks toward eternal, or supernal, things, Psalm 24: 'my eyes are ever toward the Lord. As the eyes of the handmaid are on the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes unto the Lord our God,' and so on.

bibl.author: Vita sancti Martini Turonensis Sulpicii Severi

cit.quote: Such was blessed Martin, of whom it is found in his Life: 'his eyes and hands always intent upon heaven, he never relaxed his unconquered spirit from prayer.'
Such were very many in the desert of Egypt, as Jerome sets forth in the Lives of the Fathers.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the forty-third place, that fish called the flying fish is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so named because it flies over the waters; and as often as it is seen flying outside or above the water, it signifies a coming change of weather.

It signifies men who lift their affections, above the mind, beyond the desires of this age, who, doing so, by their upward-active prayers and devotions, remove the storms of temptation from themselves and from others, 2 Corinthians 5: 'for whether we be transported in mind, it is to God; or whether we be sober, it is for you; for the charity of Christ presses us.'
Chrysostom, On the Praises of Paul: 'thus Paul walked on earth, as though he enjoyed the company of angels in heaven. For, though confined in prison, he dwelt in heaven.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the forty-fourth place, that fish called the 'squatus' (angel-shark) is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so named 'because it is sharp with scales; whence also its skin is used to polish wood.'

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Moralia in Iob Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: The limbs of Behemoth are the devil's demons, its body 'joined together with scales pressing one upon another,' that is, mutually inflaming one another and sharpening, or instigating, or provoking one another to evil, as is found in the mystery of Job 40, and blessed Gregory explains in the Moralia.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the forty-fifth place, that fish called the 'sar' is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For, abounding in Syria near the city of Tyre, which formerly gave the city the name Sara before it was called Tyre, from this the small fish of this kind, resembling it, are called sardines, or 'sardae.'

It signifies those who, abounding in holy offshoots in a congregation or homeland, give a good name to the whole nation, and this good name, passed down to many other dearest sons, draws and begets them for God, as they invoke and follow, in imitation, their merits and the renown of their fame: 'for in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I have begotten you. We are the good odor of Christ unto God.'
Ambrose, in the sermon On a Bishop Confessor: 'how great is the glory of one who rejoices in the wisdom and devotion of so many sons.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the forty-sixth place, that fish called the dogfish is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is 'so named after land dogs, because it bites,' and, as is known by experience, these fish attack others.

It signifies wicked or presumptuous men, reprovers or even discussers of others' good deeds, either denying them or arrogantly ascribing them to themselves, Micah 3: 'they bite with their teeth, and preach peace; and if any man gives not something in their mouth, they sanctify a war against him.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis De consideratione ad Eugenium papam

cit.quote: 'They have taught their tongues to speak great things, while their deeds are trifling. Most lavish promisers and most sparing performers, most flattering adulators and most biting detractors.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the forty-seventh place, that fish called the cuttlefish is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so named because 'it is more easily caught when hemmed in among enclosures.' In mating it is an obscene kind; for it conceives through the mouth, like the viper. Its ink is of such power that, some relate, added to a lamp, it makes the Ethiopians visible, once the former light is removed.

It signifies that sinners, entangled in wickedness, are more easily caught by demons and led down to hell, according to that saying, Proverbs 5: 'his own iniquities catch the wicked, and he is fast bound with the ropes of his own sins.'
It signifies also those deep and eager in lust against nature, of whom the apostle speaks, Romans 1.

bibl.author: Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Corinthios secunda

cit.quote: It signifies also the sin of the art of necromancy, the god of this world withdrawing from the faithful the light of heaven, and bringing in its place blindness of mind and a vision of demons, according to what the apostle says: 'in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers, that the light of the Gospel should not shine unto them.'

Among such was blessed Cyprian the martyr, before he was converted to the way of blessed justice, who, for the scholar Agladius, out of a shameful love for him, by his magic art invoked demons and sent them to tempt her, and procured her seduction with great zeal, as is found in the Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the forty-eighth place, that fish called the squid is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For 'in the ocean off Mauritania, not far from the river Lixus, it is said to fly out of the water in such multitudes of its kind that they can even sink ships.'

They signify the creeping things — the immense number of demons and heretics rising up out of the world, or within the world, for the drowning both of churches and of religious, and of all souls, or of each single soul, Psalm 103: 'so is this great sea, which stretches wide its arms; there are creeping things without number.'
Ambrose, in the sermon On a Bishop Confessor: 'let us, therefore, resist the manifold temptations of this world by chastity and chaste deeds.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the forty-ninth place, that fish called the eel is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For its likeness to the serpent gave it its name, and 'its origin is from mud; whence, when it is caught, it is so slippery that the more strongly you grasp it, the more quickly it slips away. They say that the river Ganges, in the East, produces eels three hundred feet long. If eels are drowned in wine, whoever drinks of that wine afterward has no distaste for wine.'

It signifies certain cunning and malicious men, sprung and rooted, after the manner of demons, in the love or lust of earthly things, whom, when a man thinks he knows and holds fast, he then knows and holds the least. Some of these are of such excessive malice and deceit that they are a singular wonder to those who discern them. Yet some of these, once converted, and, in the fervor of grace, dead to the world, become an example to others, and remove their spiritual distaste.

Among such was Elymas the sorcerer, Acts 13, who, according to Paul's own testimony there, being full of all subtlety and mischief, an enemy of all justice, was, by divine judgment, at Paul's command, struck blind, and, according to some, believed; and Sergius Paulus the proconsul, seeing this, believed, marveling at the teaching of the Lord. Augustine likewise gives a similar example, in the book of the Confessions, of Victorinus, the great orator of the city of Rome, who had deserved a statue in the Roman forum, and who, converted and publicly professing the faith, was an example and a joy to all who wished to be saved and who found themselves in a similar or comparable state.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the sea-dragon is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For 'it has spines on its gills, pointing toward its tail, which, when they strike whatever they encounter, pour out venom'; whence it is so named for this reason.

It signifies the devil, or heretics, who, with the barbs of temptations or heresies, infect and utterly corrupt with the venom of sin, or the leaven of error, whomsoever they strike: 'put away the evil one from among yourselves. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?'

An example is found in Nicholas, the newcomer from Antioch, who, as is found in the Tripartite and Ecclesiastical History, inspired by the devil whose servant he was, infected and corrupted an entire nation by his error. For he taught that wives could lawfully, and without sin, be exchanged among other men for their beds. And, though this accursed man had a beautiful wife, as the worst of apostates he did what he taught, so as more easily to encourage others to believe him; and so it came to pass.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: That fish called the torpedo-fish, which the Romans call 'serpigo,' is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For it is so called 'because it makes the body grow numb if one touches it upon the belly.'

Pliny also relates that, if touched by a spear or a rod, it makes even the strongest arms grow numb, and however swift the feet for running it can bind them; so great, indeed, is its power that it affects the limbs even through the very breath of its body.

Second, it signifies the devil, or a very proud man, who, greatly indignant at wrongs done to him, especially those that touch his heart, takes away, if he can, the power of doing good. And if he is checked by adjurations and prayers, or by the authoritative commands of the saints, he plots and strives, as much as he is able, to avenge himself, and to weaken those who do such things in their spiritual strength, and to bind and shackle those who proceed swiftly toward God in holy affections.

His wickedness is of such venomousness that he affects the inner parts of the one tempted merely by suggestion, stirring up desires, if that man consents or agrees to his suggestions, Job 41: 'there is no power upon earth that can be compared to him, who was made to fear no one. He beholds every high thing; he is king over all the children of pride. Out of his nostrils goes forth smoke, like that of a pot heated and boiling. His breath kindles coals.'
Thus it is said of the devil, that he is a lion and a dragon: a lion for his onslaught, a dragon for his ambushes.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the fifty-second place, that great fish called the 'musculus' (mussel-fish) is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For 'the whale is said to conceive by mating with it'; whence it is called 'musculus,' as the same author says, as it were the male of the whale.

It signifies spiritual men, great in virtue, prelates in the Church, begetting, from the Church entrusted to them, good and great sons for God most high and for the Gospel of Christ: 'for in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I have begotten you.'

bibl.author: Bernardus Clarevallensis Sermones super Cantica Canticorum Bernardi Clarevallensis

cit.quote: Notice that in spiritual marriage there are two kinds of bringing forth, and from this different, though not opposed, offspring, since holy mothers bring forth spiritual understanding, whether by preaching to souls or by meditating.

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the fifty-third place, those fish called the shellfish mussels are of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For 'oysters conceive from their milk.'

They signify that spiritual men, and especially religious, who, after the manner of oysters, dwell enclosed in cloisters, conceive from the milk of the apostles' teaching, 1 Corinthians 3: 'I have given you milk to drink.'
1 Peter 2: 'as newborn babes, desire the rational milk without guile, that thereby you may grow unto salvation.'

Augustine, book 7 of the Confessions: 'your Word, Lord, was made flesh, that your wisdom, by which you made all things, might give milk to our infancy, and that we, seeing your divinity brought low before our feet, might fall down, prostrate before it; and that he, rising, might lift us up.'

bibl.author: Isidorus Hispalensis Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: In the fiftieth place, that fish called the 'umbra' (shadow-fish) is of this condition, according to Isidore, book 12. For fish of this kind are so called 'because they are the color of a shadow.'
