They signify certain hypocrites who, on account of the disfigurement of their faces and expressions, seem and are, as it were, mere shadows in the Church, or in religion, or in the family; against which, Matthew 6: 'when you fast, be not, as the hypocrites, sad; for they disfigure their faces,' and so on.

Augustine, On Christian Discipline: 'let not your heart be at variance with your face; do not have your face turned upward while your heart is turned downward. How do you deserve that God should turn his face away from your sins, if you yourself do not turn your face away from your own sins?'
That great fish called Leviathan, Job 3 and 40, and Isaiah 27. If, as certain glossators say, it is the whale, there is no need to say more, since it has already been treated fully above.

But if it is the greatest sea-serpent, a bolt and crooked, as though undeceivable and incomprehensible, as seems to be implied in Job 40 and Isaiah 27, where it is said: 'in that day the Lord shall visit with his hard, and great, and strong sword upon Leviathan the bolted serpent, the crooked serpent,' and so on.
So, according to the Gloss there, because it is interpreted as 'their addition.'

It signifies the devil, who is indeed so called 'because, after he has brought in evil guilt by evil suggestion, he does not cease daily to increase it by evil persuasions. For in his crookedness a flowing softness is marked, but in the bolt a hard rigidity. So, that it may signify him both hard and soft, it names him both bolt and serpent. For he is hard through malice and soft through flattery. He is called a bolt because he strikes even unto death. He is called a serpent because he pours in his snares softly.' Thus far the Gloss.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the fifty-sixth place, that fish called the sturgeon is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, being of precious flesh and flavor, it has strong and sharp scales, an elongated head and tail, but a thick and fleshy middle. Whatever it has in it is pleasingly fit for human food, except for the scales.

It signifies grave and learned men in the Church who, being of precious life and edification, are fortified with virtues and sharpened by the goads of divine zeal; they have a mind expanded toward God and a long-suffering perseverance; but an affection enlarged with charity and full of piety, and all that they live, feel, and know is of profit to the churches of Christ and to individual souls.
Such were Peter and Paul, as is clear from their letters and from the Acts of the Apostles.

Such were Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory, who, excelling in the preciousness of their life and in the example of their edification, were virtuous men and zealots in the Church. They also had minds that acted upward, and stood out in long-suffering perseverance, and had affections enlarged with charity and full of piety, as is clear from their writings, and equally from the historical accounts of their deeds.

div.head: Cap. 57: De bellua siue de faste

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the fifty-seventh place, that fish called 'faste' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For water drawn into its mouth becomes sweet, and smaller fish, following it, enter its mouth, which it then suddenly seizes and swallows.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: According to the same author, there is a similar sea-monster which breathes water from its jaws with a fragrant vapor, whose smell fish, sensing it, follow, and enter its jaws for the sake of the fragrance; and this monster, swallowing them, is thus fed by them.

They signify the true preachers of the Gospel, in whose mouth the wisdom that is from heaven grows sweet, and from whose jaws breathes the fragrance of eternal life; and devout persons, sensing or perceiving this, enter, through the effect of teaching, into observance, and are thereby incorporated and carried into the womb of Mother Church, 2 Corinthians 2: 'but thanks be to God, who always triumphs us in Christ Jesus, and manifests the odor of his knowledge by us in every place; for we are the good odor of Christ unto God,' and so on. 'And for these things, who is so sufficient?'

It is sung of the eleven thousand virgins: 'in your fragrance, O Christ, thus these run to their punishments, as though they rejoiced in torments as in delights. They have tasted and seen how sweet you are, Lord, and have gladly spent themselves for your name. These are the flowers of beauty, which the springtime of breathing grace and the summer of charity have brought forth today.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the 'petrosa' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is so named from the multitude of its stone-like joints. It is a broad fish, tailed like a mouse, of cheap price and equally poor flavor.

It signifies a man bound up with the varied hardnesses of beasts of burden, spread wide toward earthly things, whose end is a beast's end, base in character and tasteless in speech and action, Psalm 48: 'man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless beasts, and made like to them.'
'How very base you have become, repeating your ways.'
'For I know that you are hard, your neck is an iron sinew, and your brow of brass.'
An example is found in Simon Magus, and in Julian the Apostate, and in Nicholas the newcomer from Antioch, of whom is found in the Tripartite and Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the lamprey is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, having a shape somewhat like an eel, though of a varied and more beautiful color on its underside, above the middle it has certain painted and graceful markings, distinct and orderly. It is precious and especially flavorful, and delicate, much accepted among kings and lords among fish, and, comparatively among the kinds of fish, wholesome for healthy men.

It signifies good men, long-suffering in hope, capable of charity, or love, for God and neighbor, and fit for virtues and the gifts of sevenfold grace, beautiful in character and distinguished by the variety of graces freely given, with grace and the edification, or consolation, of others; precious in wisdom, flavorful in eloquence, acceptable to God and angels and men, and wholesome in speech and action.
Such was blessed Stephen, as is found in Acts 6 and 7.
Such was Barnabas, as is found in Acts 9, 13, 14, and 15.
Such were blessed Nicholas, blessed Benedict, and blessed Bernard, as is clear from their deeds and from ecclesiastical histories.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the sixtieth place, that fish called the 'umbrina' is of this condition. For, according to Iorath, On Animals, it is a great fish, precious, long, thick, fleshy, flavorful, solid, fittingly fat.

It signifies, in the Church, great prelates or religious who, after the likeness of this fish, ought to be precious in wisdom, long in perseverance, thick, or full, of probity and virtue, full of piety, flavorful in devotion, and fat with heavenly anointing.
Such were, in the primitive Church, the apostles and disciples, as is found in the Acts and in the Ecclesiastical History.
Such, too, were the good shepherds who came after the apostles, as blessed Gregory tells of many, in the book of the Dialogues, and the Tripartite History names many.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Those fish called herrings are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For they are of brief measure, and flavorful, and wholesome, and plentiful, and at certain fixed times draw near to land in the greatest multitude. When their catching is at its height, they eat nothing, but live on water alone. They have a certain very long intestine, golden within, and are, moreover, most translucent and choice.

They signify men humble in habit, sweet in affection, wholesome in speech, abounding in virtues, condescending to the weak at fixed times, precisely when there is greatest need, with holy edification or instruction. They are fed, above all, on the grace of God and the venerable Scripture, and also have a long-suffering desire for golden glory. They are, no less, always open to heavenly influence, or to the rays of eternal wisdom.

Paul, and likewise blessed Ambrose, having all these qualities aforesaid, as Augustine says in the book of the Confessions, served the infirmities of men, 'and the hidden mouth that was in his heart chewed the sweet joys of the heavenly bread.'
Blessed Gregory did likewise, as is found in his Life.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the 'scorpinus' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is so named because it has rough spines. Its dwelling, moreover, is among the rocks, and therefore it is very wholesome and flavorful, in no way distasteful.

It signifies religious austere in life and full of zeal, whose way of life is in the wilderness, or in the woods. And therefore they are of wholesome edification to others, and contain and offer a heavenly savor.
Such was the venerable Baptist, as is found in Matthew 3, and Luke 3, and Mark 1.
Such was blessed Anthony the monk, as blessed Jerome sets forth in the book of the Lives of the Fathers.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the 'cochius' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, being of a reddish color and of white and firm flesh, not fatty, it is wholesome and fittingly flavorful. It has a large head in proportion to its body, and a slender, sharp tail.
It signifies a fiery man, bright with chastity, firm in constancy, not wanton in austerity, wholesome in speech, magnanimous in mind, jealous in perseverance.
Timothy, Titus, Dionysius, Clement, as is clear from their deeds and from ecclesiastical histories.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the codfish is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is great of body, white of flesh, hard to digest, fittingly firm, flavorful to the taste.
It signifies men magnanimous in mind, bright with chastity, mature or deliberate in judgment, steadfast in fairness, wholesome in speech and learning.
Barnabas, as is found in the Acts.
Gregory, as is found in his Life and gathered from his teaching.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the sixty-fifth place, that fish called the conger eel is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is called the sea-eel because of its likeness to lake-eels. It is flavorful and white of flesh, but very loose in texture, and therefore not very wholesome, especially for those prone to its ill effects.

It signifies those who apparently have the savor of truth and the brightness of chastity in the Church, or in religion, and yet do not truly have them; rather they dissolve, corrupting and fermenting whomever they find fit for it, or weak.
Such were Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom the apostle therefore delivered to Satan, as is found in 1 Timothy 1.

bibl.author: Passio sancti Tiburtii (in passione sancti Sebastiani)

cit.quote: Such was Torquatus, of whom is found in the legend of blessed Tiburtius.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those fish called 'sori' are of this condition, according to Iorath. For they are small by nature, and do not easily grow beyond the size of half a human cubit. Likewise they are of fitting flavor and wholesomeness.
They signify good laymen, humble among others, not exalting themselves, of good edification in themselves and of wholesome exhortation to others.
Such were Fortunatus and Achaicus, of whom is spoken in the last chapter of 1 Corinthians.
Such, too, was the mother of blessed Augustine, as is found in the book of the Confessions.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called 'oculatae' (large-eyed) are of this condition, according to Iorath. For they are so called because of the notable size of their eyes in proportion to their body, which is not large. This fish is quite broad in proportion to its length, delicate too, and precious, and is judged comparatively wholesome and flavorful.
It signifies a discreet and circumspect man, notably ample in charity, precious in life, and accustomed to divine consolations, wholesome and sweetening in his teaching.
Such was blessed John the Evangelist, as is clear from his Gospel and from his letters, and the Apocalypse, and his legend.
...blessed Ambrose, as he testifies in the book of the Confessions, and as is clear from his legend.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: In the sixty-eighth place, those fish commonly called 'ragiae' (skates or rays) are of this condition, according to Iorath, for they have more breadth, a tail and a beast-like shape, cheap flavor, and a very common value. And so they are food for ruffians and other base persons like them.

They signify lovers of this world, spreading themselves out only in temporal things, having a beast's life and end, lacking edification and virtue, or usefulness; wherefore they are devoured by demons.
Among such were Antiochus the Illustrious, the worst of men, of whom 1 Maccabees 9 speaks; and Herod Agrippa, of whom Acts 12 speaks.
Likewise Simon Magus and Julian the Apostate, of whom is found in the Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called 'palamitae,' or 'variati,' or mackerel, are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For they are beautifully varied in color, elongated in tail, pleasant in flavor, precious in value, quite free of harmful fatness, yet hard to digest, and for that reason held in lesser esteem.

They signify good men, adorned and graced by the variety of holy character and virtues, long-suffering in perseverance, edifying, instructing, or excelling in teaching and counsel, keeping themselves far from temporal things, doing everything with deliberation, and therefore not pleasing to wicked or light men. Among such were Moses and Samuel and the like, as is contained in the canon of the Bible.
Among such were Jerome and Gregory, as is clear from their writings.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'columbus' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, having a wholly beast-like shape, it has white flesh but of little flavor, of little value, and of much harm to those who eat it. It is therefore not in use among grave and learned persons.

It signifies certain young men, beautiful in face, beast-like in conduct, ill-pleasing to others in their actions, having little of goodness and very much of wretchedness and iniquity; and so they corrupt those familiar with them, and their doings do not please the wise and discreet.
Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah, sons of David, as is found in 2 and 3 Kings; such too were the sons of Eli the priest, as is found in 1 Kings 2.

Such were those two sons of an emperor, of whom Jerome speaks, in the Lives of the Fathers, who stretched nets in the wilderness for forty miles around, for hunting, and seized a holy old man and tried to compel him to deny the faith.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the salmon is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, being great and noble, it is handsome in appearance, reddish in flesh, delicate and flavorful to the taste, comparatively wholesome, precious in value, moderate in digestibility, famous in reputation, most ingenious in escaping the net. For, with wondrous cunning, laying its tail over its own head and leaping upward, it escapes the ambushes of fishermen with great speed and agility.

It signifies men noble in mind and magnanimous in Christ, gracious in conduct, charitable and fiery in affection, delicate and sweet in unction, or inward consolation, wholesome, in comparison with others, in learning, precious in probity, discreet in deliberation, illustrious in reputation, and most keen-sighted in cunning against demons and tyrants.
Such were the Maccabees, namely Eleazar, the eminent elder, and the seven brothers with their mother, as is found in 2 Maccabees 6 and 7.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Such were those fifteen hundred servants of God under father Pachomius, as Ambrose says, On Paradise.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the red mullet, 'trigla,' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, of short shape, it is reddish and as though suffused with gold, precious in value, delicate in flavor, and has a certain spine on its head.
It signifies those in the Church or in religion who are humble, charitable, discreet, useful, gracious, and jealous in mind.

bibl.author: Hieronymus Stridonensis De viris illustribus Hieronymi

cit.quote: Such were Timothy and Titus, as is clear in their letters; such were all the illustrious men of whom blessed Jerome makes a book.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called 'needle-fish,' from their shape, are of this condition, according to Iorath. For they have spines on the head, are elongated, suffused within with a certain fatness, drawn out with a certain greenness, of fitting length, proven in flavor and of rather common wholesomeness.
They signify zealous men, mortified in mind and face against the flesh, suffused with heavenly pleasantness, long-suffering in hope, gracious in conduct, and wholesome in common learning.
Such were Sosthenes the brother and Silas, of whom 1 Corinthians 1 and Acts 15 speak.

bibl.author: Pseudo Dionysius Areopagita Epistole Pseudo Dionysii Areopagite

cit.quote: Such were Dorotheus and Demophilus and Polycarp, to whom blessed Dionysius writes various letters, as to fellow disciples and proven familiars.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the plaice is of this condition, according to Iorath. For it is broader of body, more tender of flesh, whiter in color, precious in value, pleasant in flavor, comparatively praiseworthy in wholesomeness, and is found more useful and pleasant to eat when steeped in wine.

It signifies clerics, or religious, or especially prelates, who, after the likeness of this fish, ought to be found expansive in charity, kind in gentleness, bright with chastity, strong in probity, gracious in edification, wholesome in teaching, and steeped in the wine of the fervor of the grace of the Holy Spirit, that they may be found more praiseworthy and useful in the Church of God.
Such were the apostles and disciples in the primitive Church, as is found in the Acts of the Apostles and in the Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Such were the shepherds after the apostles, as blessed Gregory gives examples of many, in the fourth book of the Dialogues, and blessed Ambrose in the book On Paradise, and blessed Jerome in many places, and the Tripartite History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the sea-locust is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, wholly reddish in color, it is found white in flesh, armed with spines, wholly rough on the outside, hard to digest, with its head or tail much bent back; it has strong and quite piercing strikes.

It signifies a religious man wholly fiery with the love of God, wholly bright with chastity, wholly filled with the zeal of God, wholly rigid with austerity, wholly discreet in deliberation, wholly and perseveringly humble in mind and body, wholly intent upon and fighting against vices and disorders.
Phinehas and Mattathias, as is found in Numbers 25 and 1 Maccabees 2.
Blessed Jerome, as is clear in many ways from his writings and deeds.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the tuna, whence also 'tunny-meat,' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, great of body, filled in the belly with much fat, precious in value, it is found flavorful when eaten, especially if fresh. It has a large head, full of bones, a thick middle, and is covered with scales; salted and transported, it is found useful to many nations; it is somewhat hard to digest, but comparatively not unwholesome.

It signifies good Christian princes in this world who, after its likeness, are magnanimous in mind, in Christ, filled with Christian charity and piety, precious in probity, approved in conduct, fortified above the mind, fruitful and multiplied in affection, fortified and set forth in virtues, useful to all peoples, famous for edification and discretion.
Such were David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, as is found in the books of Kings and Chronicles and Ecclesiasticus.
Such were the emperors Constantine, Theodosius, and Maurice, as is found in the Tripartite History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Those fish called 'albi,' or 'albelli' (whitefish), are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For they are so named from their color; they are tasteless and of little value or power; nor are they very good by themselves, without some seasoning.
They signify certain young men or women, comely in face or form, but lacking in action or edification, showing no traces of virtue or goodness, who, left to themselves, are worth nothing at all.
Hamor, son of Shechem, who raped Dinah, the daughter of Jacob; and Dinah herself, who went out to see the women of the region, as is found in both cases in Genesis 34.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the tench is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For it is notably covered with scales, of common shape and color, of common price and flavor equally; its fat and flavor are best around the belly; it has a full, good head, a rather flavorful tongue, at certain times a wholesome fish, at certain times unwholesome.

It signifies common or middling persons in the Church, fittingly furnished with virtues, acceptably received in conduct and edification, sufficiently fed, in their affections, with heavenly sweetness or consolation, endowed with a good magnanimity in the higher part of reason, well-graced in speech, edifying at certain times, and at other times showing some defective traces from their frailty.

Such were nearly all the apostles before the coming of the Holy Spirit; such were nearly all the disciples of the fathers in Egypt, of whom Jerome writes, and also Cassian, in the book of the Conferences of the Fathers.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: In the seventy-ninth place, that fish commonly called the pike is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, fittingly great of body, and noble among the common fish of lakes, pleasant in color, it has white flesh free of harmful fat; it has an agreeable flavor, a good price, a due wholesomeness, a head or mouth very spiny, and it is thievish and voracious toward lesser fish.
...greedy persecutors of demons and evil men.
The figure of such men was borne by Joab and Abishai, sons of Zeruiah, and Amasa and Abner, soldiers of David, as is found in 2 Kings 2.
Such, too, were those who served as soldiers under the emperor Constantine, as is found in the Tripartite History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That river fish commonly called the bream is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, gracious in color, white in flesh, agreeable in fatness, plump, it is found pleasant in flavor; it is, moreover, of good price and due wholesomeness, and, no less, is well covered with scales.

It signifies nuns, gracious in conduct, bright with chastity, fed on the sweetness of heavenly fatness, especially devoted to edification, upright and discreet, wholesome in exhortation, and fortified with virtues.
Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, as is found in Luke 2.
Such, too, was the mother of blessed Augustine, as is found in the ninth book of the Confessions.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the 'scarpa' (parrotfish) is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, covered with scales good both in color and in flavor, it is commonly pleasant, and also especially fit for frying.

It signifies good widows in the Church, fortified with virtues, gracious in conduct and edification, affectionately devoted to compassion and condescension toward the weak and the afflicted. Among such was the mother of Timothy, and likewise his grandmother, as is suggested in 2 Timothy 1.
Among such, too, was the mother of blessed Gregory, and her friend Tarsilla, as is found in the book of the Dialogues.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'alloda' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, being of fitting color, flavor, and price, it is especially suited for roasting.
It signifies good married women who are of beautiful conduct, good edification, good discretion, great charity, and fervent piety toward the weak and the poor.
Such were those women who, still having husbands, followed the Lord, as is found in Luke 8.
Such, too, were the sisters of blessed Ambrose, as is said in his deeds.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'scandaua' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For it is very scaly, of quite common flavor, and better suited for frying.
It signifies women abounding in common virtues, edifying in common ways, and especially devoted to compassion for the afflicted.
Mary of Rome, Romans 16; likewise Stephana of Corinth, 1 Corinthians, last chapter.
Among such, too, were Romula and Galla and Tarsilla, of whom blessed Gregory writes in the fourth book of the Dialogues.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: That fish called the 'lachia' is of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, white in color and as though partly suffused with gold, milk-white and gracious in appearance and flavorful in taste, it is also precious and quite delicate, and of due wholesomeness.

It signifies virgins in the Church, most chaste in their senses, endowed with evangelical discretion and wisdom, milk-white with holy exhortation, gracious in conduct and sweetening in edification, delicate and outstanding with heavenly anointing, and sound in reputation.

bibl.author: Paulus Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Corinthios prima

cit.quote: Such were the virgins the apostle Paul wished for, 1 Corinthians 7, throughout almost the whole chapter.
Such virgins blessed Ambrose admonishes them to be, in the book On Holy Virginity, throughout.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'lichia' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, being great and thick and long, it is of common color, but of better flavor, good price, and good wholesomeness, comparatively.

It signifies the good nobles in the Church who are magnanimous in mind, filled with virtue, long-suffering in hope, of good conduct and great edification, precious in probity, and wholesome in speech in comparison with lesser men.
Such were Fortunatus and Achaicus of Corinth, of whom is written in the last chapter of 1 Corinthians.
Such, too, were the sons of Constantine the Great and of Theodosius, as is found in the Tripartite History.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish called the 'lasca' is of this condition, according to Iorath. For, of due proportion and better constitution, it spawns and produces milt abundantly. It is very scaly, flavorful and pleasant, and accepted by all.

It signifies good young women in a monastery or a household who, content with their own limits, are of a lovable constitution; they multiply holy conceptions, abound in the milk of holy teaching, are armed with virtues, are of great edification, and are gracious and acceptable to all.
Such was Ruth, as is found in the book of Ruth.
Rebecca, while she was young; Rachel; Abishag the Shunammite; Sarah, daughter of Raguel, as is found in their respective places: Genesis 24 and 29, and 1 Kings 1, and Tobit 3 and 10.
Such was the mother of Augustine, while she was young, as is found in the ninth book of the Confessions.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie De animalibus Iorath

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called sardines are of this condition, according to Iorath, On Animals. For, of small shape, they are pleasant in flavor, and accepted by every multitude, and are also of due wholesomeness.
They signify poor and humble religious who, by their edification and exhortation, graciously refresh the souls of the people, and are pleasing in the sight of all men.
Such were the apostles in the primitive Church, as is found in the Acts and in the Ecclesiastical History.

bibl.author: Ambrosius Mediolanensis De paradiso Ambrosii Mediolanensis

cit.quote: Such were those fifteen hundred servants of God under father Pachomius, as Ambrose says, On Paradise.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those fish commonly called 'rubiliones' are of this condition, according to Iorath. For, of short shape, they are fittingly flavorful, reddish, covered with small fins and scales, and armed with spines.
They signify the lesser ministers of churches, humbly content with their stipends, of due edification, of twofold charity, fortified with virtues, and armed with the zeal of God.
Such the apostle Paul wished clerics and all servants of God to be, as is found in 2 Corinthians 6: 'in all things let us exhibit ourselves as the ministers of God,' and so on.

bibl.author: Gregorius Magnus Regula pastoralis Gregorii Magni

cit.quote: Blessed Gregory also exhorts clerics to be such, in his Pastoral Rule.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Those little fish which the common people call 'lacterini,' or 'calcini,' are of this condition, according to Iorath. For, being of the smallest size, they are pleasant in flavor and wholesome in constitution.
It signifies a man most humble in his own estimation, pleasing to God and men by his edification and wholesome learning.
Such were Peter and Paul, as is clear from their letters and deeds.

bibl.author: Vita sancti Francisci fundatoris ordinis minorum
Vita sancti Dominici fundatoris ordinis predicatorum

cit.quote: Such, in their own way, were blessed Benedict and blessed Francis and blessed Dominic, as is clear from their legends.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: That fish commonly called the 'usio' is found to have these conditions, or properties, according to Iorath and many other great authorities. For it is a fish notable in size, beautiful in color, distinguished in nobility, lovable in flavor, honorable in presentation, and durable in preservation.

bibl.author: Apostolus Epistola Pauli ad Corinthios secunda

cit.quote: ...fish.

Second, they ought to be gracious in color, that is, in appearance and conduct, adorned with grace, according to that saying, Ecclesiasticus 50: 'as a solid vessel of gold, adorned with every precious stone.'

Third, they ought to be distinguished in nobility, that is, remarkably raised up by the nobility of heavenly teaching, according to that saying, 1 Corinthians 2: 'my speech and my preaching were not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the showing of the Spirit and of power.'

Fourth, they ought to be gracious in flavor, that is, made sweet with a supercelestial sweetness, according to that saying, Colossians 3: 'savor the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth.'

Fifth, they ought to be honorable in presentation, since, set before all persons of the world, or even before few, they ought always to be for the honor of God and of his mystery, according to the pattern of the apostle: 'as long as I am the apostle, I have honored, and will honor, my ministry.'

Sixth, they ought to be durable in preservation, that is, finally persevering and constant in all their goodness and truth and virtue, according to the example of the apostle, Romans 8: 'who shall separate us from the charity of Christ?' and so on. 'For I am sure that neither any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus.'
